title: Future Broncos: 3 Prospects to Watch in Week 11 of NCAA Football Season
summary: Welcome back to another installment of Future Broncos. Last week, I focused on a trio of defenders for Broncos Country to keep their eye on as the rest of the collegiate football season transpires. This week, I’ll switch gears and offer three players on offense since that side of the ball has been Denver’s biggest […]
full_text: CHAPEL HILL, NC - OCTOBER 03: Anthonie Knapp (54) of the Notre Dame Fighting Irish comes to the sideline after suffering a bloody nose during the college football game against the North Carolina Tar Heels on October 03, 2026 at Kenan Memorial Stadium in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. (Photo by Joe Robbins/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome back to another installment of Future Broncos . Last week , I focused on a trio of defenders for Broncos Country to keep their eye on as the rest of the collegiate football season transpires. This week, I’ll switch gears and offer three players on offense since that side of the ball has been Denver’s biggest issue in 2026. Earnest Green III — Offensive Tackle — Georgia So far this season, I’ve offered my thoughts on a handful of offensive line prospects. Mizzou’s Cayden Green, Indiana’s Carter Smith, Minnesota’s Greg Johnson, and USC’s Elijah Paige. Based on the comments section, identifying more big guys in the offensive trenches is something you are all interested in. Georgia fifth-year senior Earnest Green III has been on my radar for a while. Back in 2023, he was a fourteen-game starter for the Bulldogs at left tackle protecting future top pick Carson Beck. He continued to man down that position for nine games in 2024, but a lingering shoulder issue cost him a few games and slowed the promise he showed as a freshman. Last season, Greene (6’4″, 320 pounds) flipped to right tackle while Monroe Freeling was manning the blindside. However, he started just nine games due to lingering back issues. Though he didn’t give up a sack in the over 800 offensive snaps he played in 2005. Now healthy, Greene is back home where it all started on the left side of Georgia’s stalwart offensive line. The redshirt senior is poised to finish his collegiate career with over 40 starts and over 3,000 snaps between both tackle positions and having three different line coaches. That experience will pay off and mean a lot to NFL scouts and general managers who value experience and top-notch SEC pedigrees. I’m a big fan of the depth he gets in his pass sets. I also like his ability to anchor and hold his own against strong power rushers. Moreover, I am impressed with his ability to get up field and take on blockers at the second level. It’ll be interesting to see how he measures [arm length] during the pre-draft circuit. There are some who believe his best football is inside at guard, but I think he can stick at tackle. Last week’s performance versus Ole Miss earned him the Outland Trophy Player of the Week honors. To date, Greene has only given up four quarterback pressures on the season. The Broncos could use a tough and battle-tested player in their trenches next April, and I believe Greene (if medicals check out) has a shot at being a Day 2 selection. You can catch him in action this afternoon on ABC when the top-ranked Bulldogs host Mizzou. Anthonie Knapp — Offensive Lineman — Notre Dame For most of my Future Broncos installments, I’ve tried to focus on seniors whether it be fourth or fifth-year players. One particular reason is that NIL money has changed the NFL Draft landscape. Early declarations are basically half of what they used to be. In turn, that makes it a lot harder to find quality players to address needs. However, a potential early round pick that may wind up declaring early if he keeps playing well is Notre Dame offensive lineman Anthonie Knapp. He manned down the left tackle position for the Fighting Irish for the first 27 games of his collegiate career. For his third season, the junior has kicked inside to guard. That’s where many analysts have stated his best NFL potential might be. However, there are a handful of others who think a further kick inside to the pivot may be where he blossoms. Regardless, his versatility will be a big enhancer for his draft stock if he chooses to declare. We all know Head Coach Sean Payton values experience and versatility when it comes to offensive lineman. This Golden Domer certainly fits the bill. By the end of this season, Knapp (6’5”, 305 pounds) will have logged well over 2,000 snaps and have three full seasons of starting experience. While he could stand to put on some weight and muscle to handle the rigors of the pro game, his anchor is incredibly strong at this stage. In my opinion, he plays with NFL ready technique at the line of scrimmage. He has been an enforcer in the run game and a key reason for Notre Dame’s success on the ground this season. As a pass protector, Knapp has been credited with giving up just one sack in nearly three dozen starts. Whether or not Knapp chooses to declare remains to be seen but given Denver’s long-term needs at multiple positions on the offensive line, he would be a quality prospect for them to consider. I believe he has a legitimate shot to be a Top 50 player easily if he decides to take his talents to the NFL. You can watch him in action when the third-ranked Fighting Irish host Boston College this afternoon. DJ Vonnahme — Tight End — Iowa Thus far in our Future Broncos installments, we have highlighted just two tight ends in the 2027 NFL Draft. Underclassmen Oregon’s Jamari Johnson and Virginia Tech’s Luke Reynolds. I have a strong feeling both of them will declare and will merit early consideration by NFL teams looking to upgrade the position. This collegiate season, another underclassman from Iowa is making quite the statement this season—DJ Vonnahme. Over the years, the Hawkeyes have been a tight end producing factory under Kirk Ferentz. Players like George Kittle, Noah Fant, T.J. Hockensen, and Sam LaPorta all come to mind. Vonnahme (6’4”, 241 pounds) appears to be next to follow in their footsteps. Appearing in twelve games as a redshirt freshman in 2025, Vonnahme logged five starts and was the Hawkeyes’ leading receiver with 29 catches, 434 yards, and 3 touchdowns. He popped onto the map of scouts last season with a dominant seven catch, 146-yard performance against Vanderbilt in last year’s ReliaQuest Bowl . In eight games in 2026, Vonnahme sports 32 receptions for 314 yards and 3 touchdowns as well as one rushing touchdown. His yards per route ran (2.59) is amongst the highest in the nation. He has one of the best contested catch rates in the nation and can work multiple levels of the field. While there is no doubting his upside and talent as a receiving threat at the next level, Vonnahme’s work as a blocker leaves a lot to be desired. It’s important to note he is only 20 years old and is a former quarterback that is still learning the nuances of the position. Getting better at blocking is something he can certainly get better at with more time. Vonnahme is just a redshirt sophomore. With that in mind, a return back to Iowa seems quite likely. Though with this year’s class not having a clear-cut number one just yet, perhaps he goes pro if he gets good enough feedback in the pre-draft process. You can catch him in tonight when the sixteenth ranked Hawkeyes host Purdue tomorrow evening on NBC.

title: Detroit Lions elevate LB Owen Pappoe for Week 10 vs. Patriots
summary: The Detroit Lions announced they have elevated practice squad linebacker Owen Pappoe for Week 10 against the New England Patriots in Munich, Germany. Pappoe signed to the Lions’ practice squad just 10 days ago, after Jimmy Rolder (and eventually Jack Campbell) were placed on injured reserve. A former third-round pick of the Arizona Cardinals in […]
full_text: GLENDALE, AZ - SEPTEMBER 25: Owen Pappoe #44 of the Arizona Cardinals celebrates during an NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks at State Farm Stadium on September 25, 2025 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions announced they have elevated practice squad linebacker Owen Pappoe for Week 10 against the New England Patriots in Munich, Germany. Pappoe signed to the Lions’ practice squad just 10 days ago, after Jimmy Rolder (and eventually Jack Campbell) were placed on injured reserve. A former third-round pick of the Arizona Cardinals in 2023, Pappoe has made a career out of primarily playing special teams (49 games), but does have some experience on the defensive side of the ball as well. A highly athletic linebacker with 4.39-second speed, Pappoe can contribute in all five phases of special teams and act as an emergency option at WILL linebacker. It’s not unusual for the Lions to roster seven linebackers on game day, given how much they value special teams, and this elevation likely reflects his quick acclimation to the Lions system and ability to contribute this Sunday. That said, with running backs Sione Vaki (ankle, questionable) and Jacob Saylors (neck, not listed with a designation) dealing with injuries, and Vaki’s increased usage on offense, the Lions could certainly use a player like Pappoe to help fill gaps on special teams. We will have to wait until inactives are announced ahead of the game for more details. Of note, with the Lions vs. Patriots game starting at 9:30 a.m. ET, inactives will be announced at 8 a.m. ET.

But there are plenty more fireworks ahead in a pretty good slate of games this week. Of course, things kick off in Germany with a […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers throws a pass during the first half of a game against the Minnesota Vikings of the game at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. Lions fans will be particularly interested in the 1 p.m. ET showdown between the Minnesota Vikings and Green Bay Packers, but Kansas City Chiefs vs. Atlanta Falcons could be a low-key banger. The night closes out with a somewhat interesting Steelers vs. Bengals game, if you can stomach all the Aaron Rodgers talk. title: Dan Campbell confident Lions’ Germany travel plans will have them ready vs. Patriots
summary: The New England Patriots arrived in Munich, Germany on Thursday morning. The Detroit Lions arrived on Friday morning. Travel plans for the NFL’s ever-growing international slate have been one of the more hotly debated topics, recently ignited by the Los Angeles Rams’ expedited trip to Australia earlier in the season. They arrived the day before […]
full_text: The New England Patriots arrived in Munich, Germany on Thursday morning. The Detroit Lions arrived on Friday morning. Travel plans for the NFL’s ever-growing international slate have been one of the more hotly debated topics, recently ignited by the Los Angeles Rams’ expedited trip to Australia earlier in the season. They arrived the day before the game and left as soon as it ended. Their opponents, the 49ers, spent an entire week in Australia before the season opener. The Rams got wiped by the 49ers, 27-7, leading many to believe travel plans were at fault for Los Angeles’ lackluster performance. The difference between the Lions’ and Patriots’ approach to travel is obviously not as drastic. Twenty-four hours may not make that much of a difference, but there are bound to be some who believe the Lions didn’t take enough time to adjust. Lions coach Dan Campbell tried to assure media members in attendance in Munich that they will be more than ready for Sunday’s game. “Very confident. Very confident. I know today will be the hardest day,” Campbell said. The last 24 hours have undoubtedly been a grueling schedule for the players. Thursday in Detroit, they had a normal day of meetings, practice, and media availability. Hours later, they were on a flight to Munich, arriving around 8:30 a.m. local time (2:30 a.m. Detroit time). Using whatever energy they recaptured from sleeping on the plane, they went right into team meetings and a walkthrough practice. “We went from the plane; we have got settled in. About an hour later we have got into meetings, and you’re doing a little bit of the head bob,” Campbell admitted. Still, with over 48 hours to acclimate before kickoff, Campbell is certain the team will be more than ready for Sunday’s matchup with the Patriots. “We have got up and moved around, and I know that every eight hours here, we’re going to begin to acclimate,” Campbell said. “I know by the time we hit Sunday morning into that Sunday afternoon game, we’re going to be ready to go. So, we will be primed and ready, and I feel very good about our plan.”

title: What it’s like to witness Dan Campbell win over a room of German reporters
summary: Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell opened his Munich press conference—which was attended by nearly 100 media members—with an off-kilter story. When asked what German he’d learned from Amon-Ra St. Brown, he launched into a tale about wanting to spice up the term “spread your wings” with some good old-fashioned profanity. He wanted the f-word, and […]
full_text: Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell opened his Munich press conference—which was attended by nearly 100 media members—with an off-kilter story. When asked what German he’d learned from Amon-Ra St. Brown, he launched into a tale about wanting to spice up the term “spread your wings” with some good old-fashioned profanity. He wanted the f-word, and when he looked it up, the closest he got was “scheiße”—the word for shit. He went for it, essentially saying “spread your shit wings.” For us who know Campbell, that kind of clunky story is part of his self-deprecating charm. It’s undeniably funny, but it didn’t really land with the German crowd. They were either unprepared for the untraditional cadence of Campbell, or something got lost in translation. However, for the next 20 minutes, I was able to witness what is truly a joy every time I get the opportunity to do so: watching Dan Campbell win over a room. As the mostly German press got a crash course on Campbell’s folksy accent and imperfect diction, they were also treated to his charm and authenticity. My attention quickly turned from Campbell’s answers to the media members consuming his words. The cracked smiles that eventually gave way to unstoppable laughter. The nods of shared experience. The realization by some that they better get their phones out before this incredible answer ended. There were two answers in Friday’s press conference where Campbell shined the most and left the crowded pub-turned-media room beaming. The first was when Campbell was asked about making his pitch for an international fan to become a Lions fan. Campbell, instead, made an entire argument for the game of football. Campbell, as he often does when he’s about to drop bars, took his time to really think it through before answering. “I was fortunate enough to be able to play this game before I coached it. I got to play 11 seasons. I think this is my 28th year in the NFL. I think it’s 28,” Campbell said, as he ramped up the passion. “This game, this game gave me a life, okay? I was not a superstar. I was not a speed demon. I’ve got size. I played tight end, so you do a little bit of everything. But it gave me an opportunity to make a life and do something I absolutely loved with a group of guys—at any given time, 53 men that have the same goal, and you’re all going in the same direction, and the blood and the sweat and the tears that it requires on a daily basis to be great are things you never forget.” Buckle up, he’s just getting started. “And it builds character. It builds character in your team, it builds character in your individual, and it allows you overcome anything in life that may come your way. I tell the team all the time, one day you’re going to get hit; you’re going to get rocked with something really tough in your life. And I hate to say it, I don’t want it to happen, none of us do, but you will. And you’re going to have to be the rock, but you’re going to know how to overcome it, and you know who you can lean on, too: your brothers who have gone through everything you’ve had to go through here.” Campbell then snapped out of his own trance, as he often does after a long, passionate answer. “I just think it’s special that way. And it gives guys an opportunity that may not have all the bells and whistles—just because they do all the little things right and they maximize everything that they have in their ability.” Now drive it home with some humbleness. “That’s the best way I could do it or say it.” The NFL may as well cut that answer together right now, and play it at every event in which they’re trying to grow the game. But Campbell wasn’t done. Then he cut a promo specifically about the city of Detroit and how it has shaped his football team. “We don’t have the beach. We don’t have all this—now the summers are unbelievable, but things come a little bit harder out in that area,” Campbell said. “I always equate it to: it’s people that’ll do anything for you. They’d give you the shirt off their back if you needed it. And they’re all about doing the hard stuff. “And when I came to Detroit to take over as head coach, man, I wanted to build a team that they could relate to. We want to be a team that they can look at and say, ‘I respect that. I respect the way they go about their business.’ That there is something gritty about it. It is hard work. It is inspiring football. It’s not the easy way out.’ “And so those are really the type of fans we have, man. Just good, wholesome people that really care about each other. They put in good days’ work and man, they back us up and support the heck out of us, and we love them to death.” Throw some dramatic music behind that, play it before kickoff at Ford Field, and welcome the thousands of German fans who are now ready to ride with Detroit. Campbell’s German may not go beyond “guten tag” and “scheiße,” but there is something he shares in common with the country’s culture. And he was sure to mention it in his perfect press conference dismount. “You don’t come to Germany without getting a German beer. I know that. So, I will definitely have a beer before I leave, that’s for sure. I don’t know which one or what, but I’m getting one.” After the dust has settled, a German reporter gleefully turned to the local Detroit beat writers and asked a question we’re accustomed to answering in the States. “Is he always like that?” Yes. Yes, he is.

title: Lions vs. Patriots: 3 key matchups for Week 10
summary: It’s Germany week as the Detroit Lions (6-2) travel abroad to take on the New England Patriots (5-4). Buckle up. It is about to be a wild 11-day gauntlet as the Lions play the Patriots, Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and the Chicago Bears in that span. Meanwhile, the NFC North is absolutely insane. I love it. […]
full_text: Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff is hit by Miami Dolphins edge rusher Chop Robinson (44) during the first half at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. Right tackle Blake Miller blocks. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co It’s Germany week as the Detroit Lions (6-2) travel abroad to take on the New England Patriots (5-4). Buckle up. It is about to be a wild 11-day gauntlet as the Lions play the Patriots, Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and the Chicago Bears in that span. Meanwhile, the NFC North is absolutely insane. I love it. This is how it was always meant to be. This is adversity. Turn on local Detroit radio, and you’ll likely hear voices of doubt and concern. Switch to national outlets, and you’ll hear the Bears declared the favorites in the NFC, Jordan Love MVP discourse, and Kirk Cousins transforming the Vikings’ outlook as contenders. I love it. This is how it was always meant to be. With a win on Sunday, the Lions will take over the top spot in the NFC North with the Chicago Bears on their bye. In that event, the Lions will be 7-2 and 2-0 in the division, whereas the Bears will also be 7-2, but 0-2 in the division. All signs point to an absolute battle on Thanksgiving, as Ford Field will undoubtedly, again, welcome Ben Johnson with echoing boos. But first, taking care of business against the Patriots and Buccaneers is priority one. Three key matchups. Three opportunities to control the division. Blake Miller vs. Gabe Jacas The first key matchup is rookie versus rookie. New England’s second-round pick, EDGE rusher Gabe Jacas, Illinois, has been a disruptive playmaker from the start. For Grit Index followers, his name is not new. Jacas was one of the guys we were pounding the table for here, leading all EDGE rushers with a 9.14 Grit Index score. The Lions went with Derrick Moore, to my surprise. But an uncertain knee injury for Jacas became known after the draft process that may have been one of the contributing factors for the Lions to favor Moore. Jacas’ early play has been impressive both as a pass rusher as well as a run defender. #Patriots rookie EDGE Gabe Jacas continues to flash on tape. His sudden movements to shed run blocks like he does in the first clip with a swim move are impressive. Also showed good burst to close the pocket as a looper on a stunt for a sack. pic.twitter.com/kagHHFv8fg — Evan Lazar (@ezlazar) November 2, 2026 He plays violently with a relentless motor. The Gabe Jacas film is so good, guys. #Patriots rookie winning with power, quickness, bend around the arc and play recognition. High level stuff. pic.twitter.com/s9i2ZJab3d — Evan Lazar (@ezlazar) October 23, 2026 On the other side, however, the Lions have had a strong start from right tackle Blake Miller, who has had more ups than downs in his rookie campaign. Last week, however, was notably more down than his average performance. Blake Miller is having a hard time with the Dolphins edge speed on pass rushes — Erik Schlitt (@erikschlitt) November 8, 2026 When Jacas is lines up over Miller, my eyes will be on how the Lions’ rookie tackle responds. It will be an entertaining matchup, for sure, but also the winner of it will have a say in which team has a better flight back across the Atlantic. Christian Mahogany vs. Christian Mahogany The next matchup is all between the ears for left guard Christian Mahogany. After a benching for breaking team rules last week, Mahogany is back in the starting lineup . It became apparent watching the game against the Miami Dolphins that the Lions’ best five along the offensive line includes Mahogany, as Miles Frazier’s struggles impacted the Lions’ typically potent offense. “Look, if you say you’re gonna do something, you better hold up to it, otherwise you’re gonna lose respect of the people around you,” said Dan Campbell on 97.1 The Ticket . “Because if I’m sitting in that seat and I say one thing and then I don’t do it, I would immediately lose respect for that person. So we stick by what we say we’re gonna do here.” It is time for Mahogany to take the next step as a professional. He knows it. Lions guard Christian Mahogany did not shed light on what team rules he broke, but talked about being benched last Sunday. "I have to grow up," he said. "I let my teammates down, I let my organization down, and it won't ever happen again." pic.twitter.com/hx7ZhCRkMZ — Brad Galli (@BradGalli) November 11, 2026 The time is now. If not now, Dan Campbell surely will not let one player hold the rest of the team back. Patriots’ rookie cornerbacks vs. Lions receiving corps With veteran cornerback Carlton Davis III already ruled out for the game , the Patriots will be leaning on two rookies to play the role opposite Christian Gonzalez. The two rookies are fifth-round pick Karon Prunty, Wake Forest, and undrafted free agent Channing Canada, TCU. Following up on an abysmal performance against the Green Bay Packers’ paper tiger deep passing attack , the New England secondary will face an even more difficult matchup against the Lions. Following Jared Goff’s first game of the season without a passing touchdown and back-to-back games with an interception, ending his early-season streaks, Goff will be looking to right the ship against the Patriots. If I were a betting man, an Amon-Ra St. Brown anytime touchdown in his home country of Germany may be the safest bet of the weekend. Three key matchups. Three opportunities. Drei Schlüsselduelle. Drei Gelegenheiten. (Thank you, Google Translate).

title: NFL predictions: 4 keys to a Lions victory over the Patriots in Week 10
summary: The Detroit Lions (6-2) and New England Patriots (5-4) will face off in a Week 10 interconference battle in Munich, Germany. “We understand the challenge here,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said of the Patriots. “It’s a very good team. It’s a competitive team. They’re going to clean up a lot of things, and we’ve got […]
full_text: Nov 12, 2026; Munich, Germany; The jerseys of Detroit Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson (97) and wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (14) and New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye (10) at the Galeria Munchen Marienplatz. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Detroit Lions (6-2) and New England Patriots (5-4) will face off in a Week 10 interconference battle in Munich, Germany. “We understand the challenge here,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said of the Patriots. “It’s a very good team. It’s a competitive team. They’re going to clean up a lot of things, and we’ve got to be ready to go.” This week’s prediction preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook , who currently have the Lions listed at +1600 to win this year’s Super Bowl and are currently 2.5-point favorites in Week 10 . Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will earn a victory over the Patriots in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint. Patriot s base scheme For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 10 preview: Breaking down the Patriots’ offensive and defensive schemes . Prediction 1: Gibbs attacks the EDGE in the run game The Lions and Patriots both have old-school coaches who are both direct or indirect descendants of the Bill Parcells coaching tree. And as you might expect, like Parcells, both coaches prioritize controlling the trenches by establishing the run on offense and stopping the run on defense. By the numbers, the Patriots’ run defense looks strong. They’re 10th in DVOA run defense, ninth in rush yards allowed per game (96.7) and per play (3.9), fifth in EPA per rush (-0.12), and third in yards before contact (0.57). Their success ties to a strong interior defensive line that can stuff the run in two- and three-down sets, featuring Milton Williams, Christian Barramore, and former Lion Corey Durden. It’s tough to find room up the gut. Complicating things even further is how the Patriots deploy the blitz. Entering this game, the Patriots blitz 40.1% of the time (6th most in the NFL), and most of those blitzes come from their linebackers and come straight down the pipe—stressing the A and B gaps. However, teams run outside on Patriots 53.8% of the time (10th highest rate) because their EDGE players are more skilled as pass rushers and can be overwhelmed in the run game. Their vulnerability shows up most in explosive plays. Currently, the Patriots allow an explosive run on 10.9% of rushing attempts (20th), have allowed 22 rushes over 10 yards this season, and average 3.31 yards allowed after contact (24th). When we flip to the Lions’ rushing attack, we can see how they match up with the Patriots’ weaknesses. The Lions run the ball on the edges 55.7% of the time (7th), lead the NFL in explosive run plays (16.5% of the time), have 33 rushes of 10+ yards (3rd), and average 3.15 yards after contact (10th). If the Patriots blitz and the Lions attack the edge, Jahmyr Gibbs will have a chance to eat. Prediction 2: Goff finds success with quick hitters and deep shots The Patriots’ defensive line is built to stop the run up the middle, create pressure off the edge and with blitzing linebackers, then deploy their secondary in nickel sets 77.7% of the time (2nd most in the NFL) and run man coverage out of it 36% of the time (2nd). While chunk yards on the ground will certainly soften the Patriots’ defense, Lions quarterback Jared Goff will likely be the key to winning this game because he matches up so well with their coverage scheme. This season, Goff has an EPA of 40.57 vs. nickel defenses (2nd highest in the NFL), a per-play EPA of 0.23 vs. nickel (4th), and a per-play EPA of 0.36 vs. man coverage (3rd). What makes it worse for the Patriots is that their coverage has been exposed in recent weeks, especially by NFC North teams. Last week against the Packers, the Patriots surrendered 372 passing yards to Jordan Love, and 308 to Bears QB Caleb Williams two weeks prior. Those struggles have shown up in their EPA numbers, too. On the season, the Patriots allow a per-pass play EPA of 0.07 (26th), but over the past four weeks, that number has plummeted to 0.35 (31st) Goff’s key will be efficiency with short routes and a willingness to test them deep. When the Patriots are in off coverage, use the space against them. When they blitz, having quick-hitter answers in the vacated space behind them will lead to yards after catch (YAC). Then, when success comes underneath with Amon-Ra St. Brown and Sam LaPorta, test them with deep shots to Jameson Williams. Prediction 3: Lions focus on stopping the run; contain Maye As mentioned earlier, the Patriots want to control the game on the ground, but their results haven’t matched their dedication. The Patriots run the ball on 46% of offensive plays (10th most) and gain 119.9 yards per game (10th), but their per-play efficiency is more middle-of-the-road. As a team, they average 4.2 yards per rush (14th), but only Drake Maye and RB3 Corey Kiner average above 4.0 yards per carry; RB1 Rhamondre Stevenson and RB2 TreVeyon Henderson average 3.9 yards per carry. We see similar results in EPA and success rate. The team’s EPA per run is -0.02 (11th), while Stevenson (-0.06) and Henderson (-0.28) fall below the average. The team’s rushing success rate is 41.8% (14th), while Stevenson is close at 40.2, but Henderson is well below at 34.6%. The high volume of run plays can make a middle-of-the-road rushing attack look better than it is, but the real catalyst skewing the numbers is quarterback Drake Maye’s mobility. Maye has carried the ball 47 times through nine games, averages 4.7 yards per carry, has a per-play rushing EPA of +0.40, and a 51.1% success rate. Aside from a poor first quarter against Bills QB Josh Allen in Week 2 (when he gained 40 of his 69 rushing yards that day), the Lions defense has done a good job handling mobile quarterbacks this season. Vikings Kyler Murray gained 35 yards in Week 8, but no other quarterback has rushed for 20 yards against the Lions defense: Jacoby Brissett had 19 yards, Geno Smith (12), Tyler Shough (8), Malik Willis (7, groin injury), and Bryce Young (3) were all held under 20 rushing yards. Defenses have deployed a spy on Maye situationally, and I expect the Lions to do the same in this game. Prediction 4: McNeill pressures the middle of the OL The Patriots offensive line has dealt with several injuries this season, and they’ve struggled to keep pressure at bay. Entering this game, they’ve allowed 141 pressures (28th) and a 42.9% pressure rate (31st). Maye has done a nice job handling the extra pressure for the most part, only taking 20 sacks (17th) with a 6.6% sack rate (18th), but it has led to him making some poor choices with the football; he is currently tied for the most interceptions in the NFL with 11. So where are the weaknesses in the line? Right up the middle. New England lost both starting guards—Alijah Vera-Tucker and Mike Onwenu—to injured reserve. Backup Greg Van Roten was injured in the one game he started, landed on injured reserve, and has only recently opened his injury evaluation window. Backup center Ben Brown was then called up to shift to guard, but he’s been dealing with an injury and has been ruled out for this game. Finally, Walter Rouse has been supplementing/rotating with Brown at left guard, but he is currently in concussion protocol. Heading into this game, Matt Pryor has started at right guard the last three games and is expected to maintain that role, but left guard is still up in the air. The Patriots likely need Rouse to clear concussion protocol or Van Roten to be activated from injured reserve and step into a starting role. Regardless of where they land at left guard, they’ll have the unenviable task of trying to block Alim McNeill. title: Remembering a Random Packers Game: The Minnesota Vikings
summary: The last time I wrote about a random game between the Green Bay Packers and Minnesota Vikings, I covered a 1999 matchup the Packers had won. The 2026 Packers proceeded to lose in spectacular fashion to open the season, and I think it’s because I jinxed them. Following that same logic, I’m using my voodoo […]
full_text: (Photo by Jonathan Daniel/Getty Images) | Getty Images The last time I wrote about a random game between the Green Bay Packers and Minnesota Vikings, I covered a 1999 matchup the Packers had won. The 2026 Packers proceeded to lose in spectacular fashion to open the season, and I think it’s because I jinxed them. Following that same logic, I’m using my voodoo magic to conjure up a win for Week 10. This week’s random Packers vs. Vikings game is the 90th meeting between the two teams, when the Packers lost 20-17 on November 21st, 2005. Entering the Game The 2005 Packers were…pretty bad! They lost WR Javon Walker to a torn ACL in Week 1, and both RBs Ahman Green and Najeh Davenport were placed on IR with leg injuries. With a 2-7 record coming into their matchup against the 4-5 Vikings, the Packers had turned the ball over 20 times already. This was a far cry from the team who had won the NFC North at 10-6 the previous year while having two WRs with 1,200+ yards (Javon Walker and Donald Driver) AND a 1,100 yard rusher (Ahman Green). The team had already lost to Minnesota by 3 points in Week 7—it was time to right the ship. On the Vikings’ side, they had recently lost starting QB Daunte Culpepper to a catastrophic knee injury. Taking his place was veteran Brad Johnson, who had the Vikings on a bit of a hot streak after two straight wins. Losing Culpepper certainly wasn’t ideal, but the Vikings were finding ways to win. Key Moments After a missed 49-yard field goal attempt by the Vikings on their opening drive, QB Brett Favre and the Packers offense responded by going 3 and out. The Vikings offense proceeded to do exactly the same thing. The first score of the game came on the Packers’ next drive after a couple of big plays, including a 30 yard pass to RB Samkon Gado, and then a 15 yard pass to WR Donald Driver in the endzone. The Vikings’ next drive ended with an interception by S Nick Collins. Things were looking up for the Packers! Just kidding. Both offenses proceeded to combine for 6 straight punts. Favre then decided enough was enough—someone needed to score! So he threw a 51 yard pick-six to CB Dovonte Edwards. With about 30 seconds left in the 2nd quarter, the gunslinger rattled off a 53-yard yard pass to Donald Driver, and the Packers found themselves with a 14-7 lead at halftime. After more unsavory play by both offenses, the Vikings tied it up 14-14 in the 3rd quarter after RB Ciatrick Fason rushed for a 1 yard TD, capping off a nearly 9 minute drive. This would be the final touchdown scored by either team. The teams proceeded to trade punts and field goals, and with 3 seconds left, Vikings K Paul Edinger nailed the 27 yard dagger. Packers lose, 20-17. Brett Favre finished the day 20 of 33 for 227 yards, 2 TDs, and 2 INTs. Tony Fisher led the team on the ground, finishing with a whopping 14 yards on 4 carries, while Donald Driver finished with 5 catches on 9 targets for 84 yards and 2 TDs. All the big moments from this game can be found here. The Outcome The Packers fell to 2-8 on the season, and would go on to win just 2 more games all year, finishing 4-12 for the team’s first losing record since 1991 (also 4-12). The 2005 Packers turned the ball over 45 times, while scoring just 31 TDs on offense. HC Mike Sherman was fired less than a year after receiving a contract extension, and the team replaced him with Another Mike™, Mike McCarthy. Their 4-12 record earned them the 5th overall pick in the 2006 NFL Draft, which they used to select LB A.J. Hawk. The Green Bay Packers and Minnesota Vikings will meet for the 133rd time on Sunday, during the day’s early slate of games at 1pm ET/12pm CT.

summary: If the Minnesota Vikings want to repeat their Week 1 win over the Packers, they’re going to have to do it shorthanded. They’ve already ruled out five players for Sunday’s game, including tight end T.J. Hockenson and linebacker Blake Cashman. Hockenson hasn’t practiced yet this week with a combination of wrist and chest injuries. His […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: T.J. Hockenson #87 of the Minnesota Vikings is tackled by Zaire Franklin #44 of the Green Bay Packers during the second quarter of the game on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images If the Minnesota Vikings want to repeat their Week 1 win over the Packers, they’re going to have to do it shorthanded. They’ve already ruled out five players for Sunday’s game, including tight end T.J. Hockenson and linebacker Blake Cashman. Hockenson hasn’t practiced yet this week with a combination of wrist and chest injuries. His absence will deprive the Vikings — and newly acquired quarterback Kirk Cousins — of one of their most productive receivers. Hockenson ranks first on the team with 35 catches and is second in yards with 328. Though he averages just 9.4 yards per catch, he’d have been a reliable and steady help for Cousins as he settles back into his familiar Minnesota environs. Cashman, meanwhile, has been in the concussion protocol all week. He leads the Vikings with 76 total tackles and is also a key part of the Vikings’ pressure scheme; his 4.5 sacks are the second most on the team, while his eight tackles for loss are tied for the team lead. The Vikings also ruled out defensive lineman Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins, wide receiver Jauan Jennings, and quarterback Kyler Murray. Though Murray’s absence is basically immaterial at this point, Ingram-Dawkins and Jennings are noteworthy. Ingram-Dawkins was a significant part of the Vikings’ defensive line rotation, playing just a hair under 58% of the Vikings’ defensive snaps this year. Jennings was more of a supporting player for the wide receiver-rich Vikings. Behind Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison, Jennings had only logged six catches in six games. But Addison also finds himself questionable for Sunday, putting the Vikings in a bit of a wide receiver bind with Jennings already ruled out. (And not for nothing, Jennings had five catches for 61 yards against the Packers in the 2023 playoffs as a member of the San Francisco 49ers. I just assume that any random role player who ever had a good game against the Packers has their number forever. It seems like it just works out that way.) In any case, the Vikings won’t be dealing from a full deck when they visit the Packers on Sunday. That’s good news as the Packers try to continue their climb toward the top of the NFC North, especially since the Packers’ injury report is anything but short as well .

title: Packers must corral Vikings return man Myles Price
summary: The Vikings’ defense is incredible. Their offense should be more capable with a new quarterback under center. But their special teams also present a very interesting challenge for the Packers. Under the guidance of new coordinator Cam Achord, the Packers’ special teams have been — with some exceptions — generally pretty solid. Pre-injury, Skyy Moore […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - OCTOBER 11: Myles Price #4 of the Minnesota Vikings runs the ball during an NFL football game against the New Orleans Saints at Cesars Superdome on October 11, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Vikings’ defense is incredible. Their offense should be more capable with a new quarterback under center. But their special teams also present a very interesting challenge for the Packers. Under the guidance of new coordinator Cam Achord, the Packers’ special teams have been — with some exceptions — generally pretty solid. Pre-injury, Skyy Moore bolstered the Packers’ return game, but the Packers’ special teams have really shined in coverage. As of this week, the Packers’ have allowed the fourth-lowest average per return on punt returns and the 10th lowest figure on special teams. (This, incidentally, aligns with the special teams stuff the Packers have historically cared about the most and done the best, but it’s still good to see them doing a good job there.) But as good as the Packers are in punt and kick coverage, the Vikings are even better at punt and kick returns. Minnesota currently ranks first in punt return average (17.5 yards per return) and second in kickoff return average (29.9 per return). It’s true the Vikings have logged a very long punt return (86 yards) and a pretty long kickoff return (68 yards), but even if you removed those long returns, the Vikings’ averages would only drop them to the fifth- and third-best spots in the league on punt and kickoff return, respectively. And it’s all thanks to return man Myles Price. Undrafted out of Indiana in 2025, the 5-foot-9, 183-pound Price was a special teams only player for the Vikings last season. He averaged a respectable 9.9 yards per return on 30 punt returns and 25.9 yards per return on 60 kickoff returns, but capped out at a long of 43 yards on his punt duties and 61 yards on kickoff returns. Certainly not bad numbers, but not eye popping. That’s changed in 2026. The pocket-sized Price leads the NFL in punt return yardage, boasts the longest punt return in the league, and is the only player in the NFL to score on a punt return this season. He’s also the only player who’s returned either a punt or a kick for the Vikings this year, meaning their impressive league-wide rankings are entirely the work of their micro machine return man. Everybody knows the Packers will have their hands full with Brian Flores, and Kirk Cousins may be enough to bolster their offense to at least some level of respectability. But if the Packers don’t take care of business on special teams, the Vikings could end up tilting the balance in that phase of the game. And in what’s expected to be a close game, any little bit could make a difference. Fortunately, special teams have never been a game-altering problem for the Packers in the past, right? Right?

Of those three players, only Jacobs played against the New England Patriots last week, and he did not finish the game. Yesterday, head coach […]
full_text: (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers have officially ruled out four players on Friday: running back Josh Jacobs (finger), edge defender Micah Parsons (knee/illness-PUP), center Sean Rhyan (ankle) and tight end Josh Whyle. Of those three players, only Jacobs played against the New England Patriots last week, and he did not finish the game. Yesterday, head coach Matt LaFleur stated that Jacobs had yet to have surgery on his fractured ring finger, but that it would be coming in the near future. The Packers used the doubtful status, which they rarely use, on linebacker Zaire Franklin, who has been out for multiple weeks with a shin fracture. He was a non-participant throughout the week’s practices. The questionable players going into Sunday’s action are: running back Chris Brooks (ankle-IR), safety Javon Bullard (ankle/knee), offensive lineman Travis Glover (knee), safety Xavier McKinney (foot), receiver Skyy Moore (ankle-IR), edge defender Lukas Van Ness (back) and guard Kevin Zeitler (ankle/triceps). In total, 9 of the active roster’s 53 players were given game statuses for this week’s action against the Minnesota Vikings, leaving just 44 fully healthy players on the roster. Considering that teams need 48 players to suit up for game days, that’s a bit problematic. My guess? The questionable players are more likely than not to play on Sunday, just because the Packers are going to need bodies — and their injured reserve designations are quickly evaporating . Already, Green Bay has used four of their eight allotted return designations this season — with the practice windows now open for Brooks and Moore. And that’s with Jacob Monk, Jonathan Ford and Warren Brinson having the potential to return this season — along with some potential moves, like Jacobs going on IR, coming down the line. The Packers already were able to withstand not having Rhyan, Whyle and Franklin on the roster in recent weeks, and Jacobs will likely be replaced by MarShawn Lloyd — who missed last week’s action — on the game-day roster. As long as the questionable players are ready to go, Green Bay shouldn’t need to shake things up too much. If they aren’t, though, their reinforcements are thin right now, and we’ll probably get a heads-up on who won’t be able to play by way of the team’s Saturday practice squad elevations. title: The Packers’ Defense Is Living on Takeaways
summary: Nine games into 2026, the Green Bay Packers’ defense has 19 takeaways: 13 interceptions and 6 fumble recoveries. Last season, they had 14 in 17 games. Sunday’s 45-27 win in Foxborough made it six straight games with multiple takeaways. Green Bay took the ball away four times and turned those turnovers into 21 points. What […]
full_text: (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images Nine games into 2026, the Green Bay Packers’ defense has 19 takeaways: 13 interceptions and 6 fumble recoveries. Last season, they had 14 in 17 games. Sunday’s 45-27 win in Foxborough made it six straight games with multiple takeaways. Green Bay took the ball away four times and turned those turnovers into 21 points. What stands out is that it isn’t coming from blitzing. Against New England, Green Bay never rushed more than four, and all three interceptions came with Drake Maye in a clean pocket. The Packers are winning after the snap, with disguise, rotation and safeties who read the quarterback. The safeties set the tone Safeties Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams have nine takeaways between them, almost half the team’s total. McKinney leads the team with five interceptions, including two-pick games against Chicago and New England. On Sunday, he picked off Maye’s first pass of the game and returned it to the New England 14. Later he read Maye’s eyes from a deep-quarter alignment and drove on a backside dig. Williams has three interceptions and a fumble recovery. His pick against the Patriots came off a Brandon Cisse deflection on a deep shot, with Williams rotating over the top while McKinney was used as a rusher. Everyone’s getting in on it Nine different defenders have a takeaway. Six of them have an interception. Isaiah McDuffie had the best all-around day in Week 9. He stepped up when Ty’Ron Hopper left with a chest injury and became the first Packer since 2000 with multiple tackles for loss, a sack, a forced fumble and a fumble recovery in one game. His strip-and-recover of Rhamondre Stevenson in the third quarter ended any thought of a Patriots comeback. McDuffie also has two forced fumbles. Javon Bullard, Zaire Franklin, Devonte Wyatt and Anthony Campbell have one each. Doing it shorthanded Green Bay has done this without its biggest name. The defense has played all nine games without All-Pro edge rusher Micah Parsons. It has also lost linebackers Edgerrin Cooper and Zaire Franklin, and three defensive tackles, to injured reserve. A defense that can’t count on pressure has had to take the ball away with coverage instead. So far it has worked: the Packers are 6-3 and have won five of their last six. Takeaway rates swing a lot from year to year, and some regression should be expected. Still, a defense whose turnovers come from disguise and safety play has a sturdier base than one living on tipped balls.
author: Rich Madrid

title: Packers Film Room: How Green Bay racked up interceptions
summary: The Green Bay Packers defense generated three interceptions with sound coverage and defense in Week 9. None came with pressure on the quarterback. In fact, all three of the New England Patriots’ quarterback Drake Maye’s interceptions against Green Bay came from a clean pocket. The Packers never sent more than four rushers and never blitzed, […]
full_text: (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers defense generated three interceptions with sound coverage and defense in Week 9. None came with pressure on the quarterback. In fact, all three of the New England Patriots’ quarterback Drake Maye’s interceptions against Green Bay came from a clean pocket. The Packers never sent more than four rushers and never blitzed, yet Maye still threw three balls to a defender who was already waiting for them. What ties the picks together is what happened after the snap. Each time, a Green Bay safety ended up somewhere Maye didn’t expect, and Maye threw to the picture he had before the snap. On the first, the single-high safety didn’t bite on play action. On the second, Evan Williams was rotating over the top of what looked like one-on-one coverage. On the third, a deep-quarter safety read Maye’s eyes and drove on the dig. Together, the three throws cost New England about 12.4 EPA, and two of them set up Packers touchdowns. The first interception came on Maye’s first pass of the game, on 2nd and 9 from the New England 26 with 14:32 left in the first quarter. Xavier McKinney picked it off at the 50 and returned it 36 yards to the NE 14, and Jordan Love scrambled in for a touchdown two plays later. At minus 5.90 EPA, it was the costliest of New England’s three interceptions. Green Bay was in a drop-8 Cover 3, rushing three with seven in the box. Before the snap, McKinney was the lone deep defender in the middle, about 12 yards off the ball, so the middle of the field was closed. New England ran play action from under center with a deep post and a deep crosser. That combination is built to stress the post safety. If he carries the post, the crosser opens underneath him, and if he jumps the crosser, the post is open behind him. McKinney never took the fake. He kept his depth and stayed square in the middle third through Maye’s drop, so the play action never created the conflict it was designed to. With eight defenders in coverage, the underneath zones were full, and neither deep route had an easy window. Maye’s eyes and shoulders stayed locked on the deep middle, McKinney read him the whole way, and when Maye threw the crosser 24 yards downfield, McKinney broke downhill and caught it in stride around the 50. Play action against drop-8 Cover 3 only works if the post safety bites. McKinney didn’t, so the ball went straight to the defender the concept was meant to beat. With only three rushers and a clean pocket, Maye had time to come off the deep routes and check the ball down. Charting graded it interception-worthy, with a CPOE of minus 42. The second interception came on 1st and 10 from the New England 40 with 12:54 left in the second quarter. Maye took a deep shot down the left sideline to Kyle Williams, 37 air yards, and Brandon Cisse batted it into the air for Evan Williams to catch at the Green Bay 23. It was the only one of the three the Packers didn’t score off, since they went three-and-out, and it cost minus 2.82 EPA. Green Bay ran a WASP quads pressure with McKinney as the fourth rusher, rotating the coverage behind him. WASP usually puts a linebacker in as the 4th rusher while dropping a defensive end. On this play, McKinney is aligned more like that inside linebacker, so he’s the one tasked with adding to the rush. New England lined up in a shotgun 3×1, with a dagger concept to the trips side and Kyle Williams isolated as the X to the boundary. Dagger uses a clear-out seam from the inside receiver and a deep dig from the outside receiver into the space the seam vacates. Before the snap, the shell looked two-high, and McKinney gave no clear sign he was coming. At the snap, he rushed, and Evan Williams rotated toward the boundary and got depth over the top of the single-receiver side. Instead of working the dagger to the trips side, Maye took the backside shot. Cisse was in phase on the go route and Williams was closing from above, so the ball landed between them. Cisse got a hand on it at the sideline, and Williams, already overhead, caught the tip. The backside go is usually a decision made before the snap: one-on-one to the X with no safety help is a throw you take. Here, though, the safety help only appeared after the snap as Williams rotated over. With a safety rushing, there were also fewer defenders underneath, so the dagger dig and the vacated middle were the coverage’s weak spots. The Packers defense made it a contested catch because Maye put too much air under it when it should have been more on a line out to the sideline. Instead, he threw a 50/50 ball into a rotating safety. The third interception came on 2nd and 7 from the Green Bay 44 with 5:47 left in the second quarter. Maye threw a backside dig to tight end Eli Raridon and McKinney undercut it at the Green Bay 29 and returned it for 2 yards. Christian Watson’s 43-yard catch and a Kaleb Johnson touchdown run followed, making it 24-7, and the play cost minus 3.68 EPA. Green Bay was in Cover 4 “trix,” a quarters variation where the weak safety reads the inside receiver from the #3 in trips. The Packers rushed four with no blitz and six in the box, and both safeties sat 12 to 15 yards deep before the snap, with McKinney on the side the ball went to. At the snap, McKinney opened to his deep quarter, but with no vertical threat from any inside receiver, he was free to read the quarterback. Maye finished his drop looking to the front side, then came back to the backside dig, with his head and shoulders turned before the ball came out. McKinney read the turn and drove downhill and inside, from deep-quarter depth to the spot where the dig would be caught, before Maye released it. The throw was on time, but McKinney jumped into the throwing lane and caught it in front of Raridon at the 29. In quarters, a safety whose inside receiver doesn’t go vertical can become a robber on in-breaking routes. Throwing a dig that late at that safety without a vertical route to hold him is exactly the throw the coverage is built to take away. Takeaways On these interceptions, the Packers only rushed three, four and four, and didn’t get any pressure on Maye, who had time and threw every one of these picks from a clean pocket. Each pick came after the snap, when a Packers safety ended up somewhere Maye didn’t expect. McKinney stayed in the middle instead of biting on play action, Evan Williams rotated over the top of a one-on-one that wasn’t, and McKinney turned a deep-quarter alignment into a robber on the dig. That’s Jonathan Gannon’s defense in a nutshell: show one picture, play another, and trust the safeties to beat the quarterback to the spot. With Micah Parsons out and the injury list growing, Green Bay can’t count on getting home with four. It doesn’t have to when McKinney and Williams are this far ahead of the quarterback. Every passer left on the schedule will see the same disguises on film, and recognizing them on tape is a lot easier than beating them on Sunday.

title: By the Numbers: Is the Packers’ offense sustainable?
summary: As I tend to do every week, I found myself talking about the Green Bay Packers a lot this week. Some of that was just muttering to myself in the hallway of my house, but sometimes I was talking to real, live people and sometimes those conversations were recorded. One question that keeps coming up […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - OCTOBER 29: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers throws the ball during an NFL football game against the Carolina Panthers at Lambeau Field on October 29, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images As I tend to do every week, I found myself talking about the Green Bay Packers a lot this week. Some of that was just muttering to myself in the hallway of my house, but sometimes I was talking to real, live people and sometimes those conversations were recorded . One question that keeps coming up has been this: is the Packers offense sustainable? On its face, the answer is “probably not.” We’re coming off a performance where Jordan Love had fire shooting from his hands: completing 79.3% of his passes for 372 yards and 3 TDs. He posted that 79.2% completion rate while bombing: 27.6% of his attempts were 20+ yards down the field (his highest rate of the season). The question of sustainability revolves around Jordan Love (“can he keep this up”), but it’s really more about the run game. Can an offense continue to be successful into the playoffs with a high pass rate and a bad running game? No matter where you look, the run game metrics are bad. They’re dead-last in EPA per Play at -0.26 (per NFL Pro ). They’re dead last in DVOA at -32.6% (per FTN ). They’re 31st in Yards Per Attempt at 3.0 (per Pro Football Reference ). Pick your favorite football analytics site and they’re going to be right near the bottom in rushing on every single one of them. In looking at the overall team, I believe it’s sustainable. On top of being an aggressive attacker down the field, Love has become a very good operator in the quick game, and the Packers have the offensive pieces to make that work. Whether that’s working an old favorite like Slant/Flat or hitting some of those quick outs he has become so fond of, it’s an area of his game that has seen a ton of improvement over the years. If they need to supplement the lack of a run game with a quick pass game – and take enough deep shots to keep defenses from sitting on the underneath routes – that feels like it could work. Combine that with a defense that has been playing extremely well (2nd most turnovers, 5th in DVOA, 9th in EPA per Play) and that feels like a recipe for sustainability. But is it really? I dug into some numbers to see if that’s something that we’ve seen before. Have we seen a team this bad at running the ball find success? I had to define success, so I determined that any team that made the playoffs could be assumed to have some sort of sustained success. So I grabbed every team that made the playoffs from 1999-2025 and looked at a handful of their metrics during the regular season to see if this is something that has happened. If you’re asking “why 1999”, the answer is because that’s the furthest back the data I am using for this goes back. The main metrics I looked at were Pass Rate, EPA and Success Rate. Here’s where the Packers sit. For these numbers, I’m only looking at games after Week 3, since the offensive line was non-functional for the first few weeks. Is that cheating? Maybe! But it felt like the best thing to do, and I’m making the rules here. We’re going to lock that Packers line so we can keep it in mind, then look at some other teams that may fit the bill. If there is a * next to a team name, it means that team was in the Super Bowl that season. First up: Pass Rate. These are the highest pass rate teams in our group. As you can see, a pass rate of 61.1% isn’t crazy given some of these other teams. It’s still relatively high – a pass rate of 61.1% would rank 97th highest out of 336 teams – but it’s not some crazy outlier. Among these teams, the Packers’ EPA per Pass far exceeds the other teams, but their running game is worse than all of them except for the 2022 Bucs. Their Passing Success is better than everyone except the 2021 Bucs and the 2011 Lions, but their running game is worse than all of them in terms of success. That led me to look at Rush Success Rate. Where does the rushing success rate from this year’s Packers team stack up against our sample? The Packers would still be a bit of an outlier – their 36.3% rush success would be the 22nd worst success rate among our 336 teams – but it has been done. The one that jumps out (because of course it does) is the 2007 Packers. I’m not alone in believing that, if they hadn’t lost to the Giants, they would have won the Super Bowl that year. For this year’s Packers to be significantly better in EPA per Pass – and slightly better in Rush Success Rate – is pretty surprising. That team also had a slightly higher Pass Rate than this year’s Packers, as well. That 2007 team had a better Pass Success Rate, so they were better at moving the chains, but this team is better at generating points. If you want to point to a volatility point, something like that would be it. A high EPA per Play but low Success Rate could suggest that a team is punching a bit above their weight. We could do this all day, but we’ll end with this. I wanted to see what teams had a Rushing EPA worse than this year’s Packers: Those are all the teams with a worse Rush EPA than this year’s Packers. A few of those teams (2022 Bucs, 1999 Lions, 2014 Colts) had a higher pass rate, but most of them were more run-heavy than this year’s Packers, despite having worse results while doing so. Of these teams, the Packers outpaced all of them in EPA per Pass and Pass Success Rate. They have a better overall Success Rate than all but 2 of these teams (2022 Bucs, 2014 Colts). We’ll stop here, or we’ll be here all day. There’s more that can be combed through, but I think we have a pretty good idea of where this Packers team stands. Let’s close by revisiting our question: Question: Is this Packers offense sustainable? Answer: History tells us that it is, but it’s also a fairly narrow path to walk. Teams with this makeup have been “sustainable” enough to make the playoffs numerous times, but it’s not the norm. Albums listened to: Blondshell – Violins ; Leem of Earth – See ; Remi Wolf – Mud

title: Green Bay Packers News: Can the Packers execute the blueprint to beat the Vikings?
summary: The Minnesota Vikings have built a truly special defense. They’re extremely disruptive and not particularly interested in letting opposing quarterbacks get comfortable. Mastermind DC Brian Flores has taken the concept of an aggressive defense to a new level, blitzing on 75.3% of defensive plays this season. The idea is to create confusion, force errors, and […]
full_text: The Minnesota Vikings have built a truly special defense. They’re extremely disruptive and not particularly interested in letting opposing quarterbacks get comfortable. Mastermind DC Brian Flores has taken the concept of an aggressive defense to a new level, blitzing on 75.3% of defensive plays this season. The idea is to create confusion, force errors, and keep down-and-distances unfavorable for offenses. And to date, it’s working. So why hasn’t anyone done this before? Well, because with aggression comes opportunities. There will be some opportunities on Sunday. Can Green Bay’s offense capitalize? I think so. Here’s how: To make Minnesota pay for sending extra defenders, Jordan Love needs to get the ball out of his hands quickly. While Love has a reputation this year for the long-developing big play, he actually has the shortest time to throw in the NFL this season (2.60 seconds). If you watched Buffalo’s win over the Vikings on Monday Night Football, you’ll have noticed that Josh Allen threw 16 passes within 10 yards of the line of scrimmage. Of those, 15 were completions, and the Bills gutted out a 23-6 win. The Packers also need the Vikings to at least somewhat respect its running game. That’s easier said than done, though the Packers did finally break 100 cumulative rushing yards against the Patriots last week. While Minnesota’s defense is bordering on generational, they rank 18th in rushing yards allowed. They’ve surrendered at least 134 rushing yards in each of their last three games. Even modest gains on early downs can help avoid the long-yardage situations where Flores’ is most aggressive. Most importantly, the Packers need to win the turnover battle. Their Week 1 loss to Minnesota was actually extremely competitive for three quarters before a late strip-sack and interception helped the Vikings pull away (I will not complain about refs, I will not complain about refs, I will not com…). While not great, Green Bay’s offensive line is much better now than it was then, particularly at pass blocking. And hopefully playing at Lambeau should make communication much, much easier. That dang horn, man. I haven’t even mentioned Cousins and the Vikings offense, because I do think the real key to this game is Jordan Love and company overcoming Brian Flores. The Packers don’t need to reinvent the wheel. Their offense works. They just need to stay balanced and focused, and recognize the pressure so they can turn it against the Vikings. The Vikings are thriving on chaos No defensive coordinator has ever blitzed as much as Brian Flores, and he’ll blitz Jordan Love with even greater frequency on Sunday. Here are the keys for the Packers. Packers’ offense vs. Vikings’ defense: What’s different from Week 1? “It’s never easy going against this defense,” QB Jordan Love says Packers slot CB Javon Bullard plans to play through injury vs. Vikings Cornerback Javon Bullard missed practice on Wednesday and Thursday due to knee and ankle injuries, but said he’s planning to play on Sunday. Matt LaFleur praises Jordan Love as MVP-worthy Love’s success this year goes beyond raw talent. His head coach explains why. Packers discussion in the Feed Is Brian Flores actually a genius? Or is he just on a hot gambling streak? Let’s talk about it! The Feed is the place for you to share whatever it is you want to talk about, big or small. title: Five good Texans questions with
summary: This week marks the second Deshaun Watson revenge game of the series. Of course, one could be excused if they aren’t quite sure who wants the revenge more. More importantly, both the Houston Texans and Cleveland Browns are in the playoff hunt in the AFC. Naturally, the Browns are in slightly better shape, but neither […]
full_text: November 20, 2011; Cleveland, OH, USA; Cleveland Browns free safety Mike Adams (20) wraps up Jacksonville Jaguars running back Montell Owens (24) at Cleveland Browns Stadium.Cleveland won the game 14-10. Mandatory Credit: Greg Bartram-USA TODAY Sports | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect This week marks the second Deshaun Watson revenge game of the series. Of course, one could be excused if they aren’t quite sure who wants the revenge more. More importantly, both the Houston Texans and Cleveland Browns are in the playoff hunt in the AFC. Naturally, the Browns are in slightly better shape, but neither can afford a loss at this point. We caught up with Chris Pokorny of Dawgs by Nature to see what we could figure out about the Browns before Sunday’s game. Battle Red Blog: The Browns have been better this season under their new coaching staff. What have they been doing differently than the old Stefanski regime? Is this something that is sustainable throughout the season? Chris Pokorny: Although it hasn’t worked as blissfully the past couple weeks, I always harp on the fact that this new coaching staff seems willing to make a lot more adjustments than the old coaching staff. I thought Kevin Stefasnki was really effective when he had an offensive line that could dominate games with a zone-blocking running scheme, and that was complemented by an aggressive Jim Schwartz defense. But over time, when the linemen were injured and past their prime, there were no adjustments to re-invent the offense; and on defense, Schwartz stuck with the same approach, even if a team ‘figured out’ out to combat it. Under Todd Monken, at least on defense, you get the feeling that there is a different gameplan and ability to make adjustments each week. On offense, Monken has been more willing to fully embrace all of his young players with boatloads of playing time. It’s been fun to see the Browns be competitive, but it’s also concerning that they haven’t had at least one game — despite an ‘easy’ schedule — in which they’ve been able to control the game with a decisive victory. BRB: The Browns appear poised to go back to Deshaun Watson after trying Shadeur Sanders. How do the two quarterbacks differ and do you think Watson gives the Browns a better chance to win? CP: When you look at his stats in last week’s game against the Saints, it looked like Shedeur Sanders did great. But if you look at things from a strategic gameplan perspective, needing to make reads, being faced with that key third- or fourth-down situation earlier in a game, Sanders still appears way to slow to process things at the NFL level. Where he succeeded was later in the game, when it was do-or-die, and the ‘gameplan’ almost goes out the window because he’s chucking it deep as he takes big hits. It worked, and honestly, that has been his strength throughout his NFL starts. It’s exciting, and I think it shows he can make the big throws at this level, but it’s also not something that is sustainable. He needs to mix that in with a much higher degree of competency on the scripted plays throughout a game, and he’s not there yet. Deshaun Watson was poor at that since signing with the Browns too, looking very skittish, but this year he’s been tremendously better at that. 3) The Browns have been a team in transition the last few seasons. Who are some new faces this year that will have a dramatic impact on the game on Sunday? They are no secret, but rookie receivers Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion lead their class in receiving yards. I can only imagine how good these guys can be when they have an upper-tier quarterback throwing their way, they are an exciting duo for fans to look forward to for years to come. On defense, I wish I could call out Jared Verse’s name as the replacement to Myles Garrett, but Verse has been a huge disappointment, ranking near the bottom of the league in metrics. I’d say that linebacker Quincy Williams, who came over from the Jets, has had a nice impact on the defense, with a few games where he borders on looking like an elite-level player (but that’s not a week-in, week-out thing). BRB: The AFC North is usually one of the more competitive divisions in the NFL. Who do you see winning the division this season? Which team in the division do Browns fans enjoy beating the most? CP: A few weeks ago, I would have thought the Browns had a solid shot since they were 2-0 in the division, had a 5-2 record, and the Ravens were beat up at quarterback. But the Steelers have shown a greater degree of consistency that I didn’t anticipate, and even though I think the Bengals’ defense has been overrated, Joe Burrow is playing at a high level, so there’s no reason to think those teams will fade. I think the Steelers’ running game being so good will allow them to win the division, along with their defense picking up the intensity. The Browns and Bengals should be contending for a wildcard spot along with the Patriots (and maybe the Texans if they gain steam). Regarding which team Browns fans enjoy beating the most in the division, I’d say it’s still the Steelers. We were so looking forward to ending our 22-game road losing streak in Cleveland a few weeks ago, but Pittsburgh blew us out there again. BRB: The Texans are favored by 4.5 points according to Fanduel. How do you see the game going? Are there any prop bets you feel comfortable recommending? CP: Especially with the Browns finally in contention at midseason for once, I’m really trying to stay optimistic with my picks each week, so keep that in mind here. The Browns have played a lot of close games, and are 3-0 at home, so this four-game home stretch that they are beginning is vital for them to stay in the playoff race. The Browns’ pass defense has remained a strong suit, but offensively, they still have some consistency issues, with too many dry stretches of scoring. Of all the games the Browns have played this season, this is the one where I feel like I have no idea what to expect. C.J. Stroud seems to be playing at an unexpectedly high level, but the Browns’ pass defense has been solid. Will Houston commit to the run, which Cleveland hasn’t been able to stop for weeks? And while Houston’s defense has struggled compared to my expectations, the talent seems to still be there, so do they get back on track against their former quarterback who takes a lot of sacks? I’ll take the Browns to win 24-21. As for prop bets, I’ll say RB Dylan Sampson over 21.5 yards receiving is a good one. He’s hit that mark in all three weeks that he’s been back from injury. We want to thank Chris for taking the time to answer our questions about the Browns. They are certainly one of the more interesting teams in the NFL so far on the season. We want to wish Chris and the Browns the best of luck for the remainder of the season. As per usual, we hope that luck begins on Monday morning.

title: The 2026 season is somehow worse than the 2011 Colts
summary: Ah, 2011. To be young again. Fifteen years have passed since then and a thousand things have changed in the NFL. History doesn’t repeat itself, but it sure does rhyme. The 2026 season for the Colts is starting to look and feel a lot like that disastrous 2011 season when Peyton Manning missed the entire […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - NOVEMBER 27: Peyton Manning and Curtis Painter #7 of the Indianapolis Colts sit on the bench in the final minute of the game against the Carolina Panthers at Lucas Oil Stadium on November 27, 2011 in Indianapolis, Indiana. The colts lost 27-19. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ah, 2011. To be young again. Fifteen years have passed since then and a thousand things have changed in the NFL. History doesn’t repeat itself, but it sure does rhyme. The 2026 season for the Colts is starting to look and feel a lot like that disastrous 2011 season when Peyton Manning missed the entire year. Somehow, some way, though, it might actually be worse. Let’s go back to where it all started. Kerry Collins was brought in off the street and proceeded to get lit up to open the season in Houston. Curtis Painter and Dan Orlovsky took it from there and produced a 2-14 season after an 0-13 start. Manning, Saturday, Clark, Addai, Garçon, Diem, Brackett, and many others were gone by 2012. It marked one of the darkest times in Colts franchise history. As dark as that season was, 2026 said, “Hold my beer.” You see, in 2012, the Colts were able to draft Andrew Luck. Remember? 2011 was the “Suck for Luck” year. There was an incredible consolation prize for being so bad. 2026? Well, it may not be as awful from a record or even on-the-field talent perspective, but it actually looks worse. Key players like Buckner, Nelson, and Downs are gone already. The departure of more names is sure to follow. Unlike the 2011 team, there is no positive mantra to pull the team through. There is no Luck coming to resurrect them. Heck, there isn’t even a first-round pick. That is what makes this year worse. It’s not about 2026 itself. It’s about the long-term effects. The future is murky. After 2011, there was a direction and goal during the season. This season sees the Colts treading water, or worse, drowning. Many more questions linger over the Colts now than in 2011. To make it worse, the answers aren’t as clear either. 2011 was a gut punch for a fanbase that was used to high-level winning. Watching Manning and others walk out the door was enough to make a grown man cry. There was hope and a direction forward, though. This year, 2026? What are we working towards? Where is the hope? What is the future? A stockpile of draft picks and Jonathan Taylor is about all there is to be excited for. From “Suck for Luck” to “Sucks to Suck,” 2026 seems to be worse than the worst Colts season in recent memory.
