summary: While Kirk Cousins exceeded expectations as the Las Vegas Raiders’ starting quarterback, getting the team to a 4-5 record and in the playoff mix at the halfway point of the season, Week 10 against the Seattle Seahawks will be the official start of the Fernando Mendoza era in Las Vegas. John Spytek, Klint Kubiak and […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images While Kirk Cousins exceeded expectations as the Las Vegas Raiders’ starting quarterback, getting the team to a 4-5 record and in the playoff mix at the halfway point of the season, Week 10 against the Seattle Seahawks will be the official start of the Fernando Mendoza era in Las Vegas . John Spytek, Klint Kubiak and the Raiders’ coaching staff determined that the rookie is ready for action, trading Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings for a third-round pick and naming Mendoza the starter. That creates plenty of excitement throughout the organization and fanbase. However, the No. 1 pick’s first start couldn’t have come against a much tougher opponent. Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald has a reputation as a “defensive mastermind”, running a scheme that has a lot of moving parts and can create confusion for opposing quarterbacks, both from a pressure and coverage standpoint. For example, Seattle’s defense ranks first in yards per game allowed ( 244.2 ), tied for fourth in points per game (18.0), tied for third in EPA per pass (-0.17) and 13th in pressure rate (39.6%), according to Sumer Sports , this season. Also, Macdonald is 6-0 during the regular season against rookie quarterbacks, partly because even veteran signal callers can have a tough time deciphering his defense. But the 2025 Heisman Trophy winner will have some help. Kubiak should be able to prepare him for what type of looks he’ll face on Sunday since Kubiak worked for Macdonald last year as the Seahawks’ offensive coordinator. Additionally, having a unique offensive weapon who can bail quarterbacks out in Brock Bowers, as well as quality check-down options in Michael Mayer and Ashton Jeanty, gives Mendoza a few security blankets to get out of trouble. There’s probably going to be some ups and downs on Sunday — and likely for the rest of the season, for that matter. But if the rookie looks sharp against arguably the best defense in the league this weekend, that should give him a lot of confidence moving forward and bode well for the Raiders’ future. So, for this week’s game day discussion on The FEED , we’ll be keeping tabs on how Mendoza looks in his first start. The game kicks off at 1:05 p.m. PST and will air on CBS (check your local listings). I look forward to talkin’ some ball with y’all!

title: Raiders Week 10: Seahawks’ Jaxon Smith-Njigba a supreme challenge
summary: Twice. That’s the exact amount of times Jaxon Smith-Njigba has been limited to under 100-yards receiving in the nine games the Seattle Seahawks have played this season. With 71 receptions for a league-leading 1,036 yards and nine touchdowns, the 6-foot, 197-pound 24-year-old is arguably the best wideout in the NFL. To say the Las Vegas […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Twice. That’s the exact amount of times Jaxon Smith-Njigba has been limited to under 100-yards receiving in the nine games the Seattle Seahawks have played this season. With 71 receptions for a league-leading 1,036 yards and nine touchdowns, the 6-foot, 197-pound 24-year-old is arguably the best wideout in the NFL. To say the Las Vegas Raiders defense will have its hands full with Smith-Njigba in Sunday’s Week 10 matchup with the Seahawks this Sunday is an understatement. Defensive coordinator Rob Leonard knows JSN presents a supreme challenge for Las Vegas and he expects Seattle to exploit any and all matchups. “Yeah, I mean, he’s unbelievable. He’s number one in the league across the category in all things, receptions,” Leonard said when asked about the collective effort it’ll take to limit Smith-Njigba. “But yeah, it’s very critical. You start with him day one. We’re still talking about him all the way, early down, third down, red zone. Not just coverage-wise, different things that we have to do.” Fully expect the Raiders secondary to get the full JSN experience with cornerbacks Eric Stokes, Darien Porter, Jermod McCoy, Taron Johnson and Hezekiah Masses to get the responsibility of covering the Seahawks elite wide receiver. This is because Seattle isn’t shy about deploying their elite wide receiver in both slot and outside alignments. The 20th pick in the 2023 NFL Draft has been a strong slot receiver since he arrived but he’s spending more time as a perimeter option, too. Now JSN hands out a stiff arm and gets down inside the 10! AZvsSEA on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/JOYUx3HZ6L — NFL (@NFL) November 8, 2026 That slot and boundary capability has truly expanded Smith-Njigba’s effectiveness and the Ohio State product’s production highlights just how much more dangerous he’s become as a weapon in the Seahawks offense. And all this despite Seattle’s offensive attack not being at the level that current Raiders head coach and play caller Klint Kubiak produced when he was the Seahawks offensive coordinator during the team’s Super Bowl-winning run last season. Rookie offensive coordinator Brian Fleury has Seattle’s offense ranked 18th in points scored (202) and yards gained (2,950). The passing game is ranked 17th in yards gained (1,953) and touchdowns scored (15) while the run game is 18th in yards gained (997) and 20th in touchdowns scored (seven). But whether it’s Sam Darnold or Drew Lock at quarterback, JSN Interestingly enough, however, Smith-Njigba’s lowest output of the season was last Sunday in a Week 9 tilt with division foe Arizona Cardinals: 10 targets, seven receptions, for 51 yards (long of 18) and no touchdowns. Leonard and the Raiders defense meticulously studying the way the Cardinals covered the Seahawks elite pass catcher in round two of their NFC West contests this year. And one of the defensive tactics Arizona deployed is something Leonard is keen to do with his Las Vegas defense: Zone-heavy and two-high safety looks. While Leonard has deployed more man coverage to try and mitigate defensive woes, returning to a zone-heavy look helps Stokes — who excels in Cover 3 and struggles mightily in man-to-man — and allowed Arizona to bracket Smith-Njigba over the top and took away the deep and intermediate routes where Seattle’s wideout does a lot of his damage. Doing this forced working underneath with shorter passes and this is an area where linebackers Nakobe Dean and Quay Walker operate, offering the opportunity to hit JSN — hard. The Cardinals’ adjust gameplan severely limited Smith-Njigba and was a far cry from their Week 2 contest where the wideout produced 155 receiving yards and three touchdowns on nine receptions. 🔥 Jaxon Smith-Njigba should be the Offensive Player of the Year! Just look at his INSANE Week 2 performance against the Cardinals! 🤯 🎯 9 Receptions 🏃 155 Receiving Yards 🏈 3 Touchdowns 📈 42.5 PPR Points JSN deserves to be the OPOY favourite! Do you agree? 👀🏆 https://t.co/U5j3YEe8HC pic.twitter.com/FdHWs5axRb — Fantasy Films (@FantasyFi1ms) November 12, 2026 To put it plain: The Raiders approach to JSN should be similar to what defenses do when matching up with Las Vegas tight end Brock Bowers — bracket and make other pass catchers beat you. But what a coverage responsibility and experience Smith-Njigba presents to the younger Raiders cornerbacks like Porter, McCoy and Masses. That trio are 25, 21 and 22 years of age, respectively, and going against one of the game’s best wide receivers should be a welcome task, albeit, daunting. According to Pro Football Reference , Porter is charged with 24 targets allowing 13 receptions (54.2 completion percentage) for 201 yards and one touchdown. Masses has been targeted 31 times allowing 16 receptions (51.6 percent) for 258 yard and a team-leading four touchdowns allowed, while McCoy draws six targets allowing four receptions (66.7 percent) for 63 yards and one touchdown. “Yeah, he’s playing faster. His eyes are in the right spot, and he made a play on the ball, which was awesome,” Leonard said when asked what he’s seen from McCoy this season. “Him and Zeke (Hezekiah Masses) are both growing, and that’s what you’re looking for, is improvement, right? So, it’s been fun to get him more reps so he can feel a little bit more calm out there.” JSN’s elite ability to maintain consistent speed through his routes without telegraphing or slowing down will thoroughly test the entire Raiders secondary’s skillset — beyond the cornerbacks, too. Because Seattle will place their elite pass catcher all over the alignment, even in the backfield and alongside an offensive tackle to truly force the opposing defense’s hand. And if Dean or Walker draw coverage responsibility based on JSN’s alignment and pre-snap motion, good luck, Raiders. At that point, the pass rush and coverage need to combine so disruption of or taking down the quarterback means no dice for Smith-Njigba. Head-to-Head Sunday’s tilt in Allegiant Stadium marks the 57th time the Raiders and Seahawks square off. The Silver & Black lead the all-time series 30-26 (29-25 in regular season play, 1-1 in postseason action). The last time the two teams played one another was in 2022 with Las Vegas dropping Seattle 40-34 in overtime on a walk-off 86-yard run by running back Josh Jacobs. Before that, the Seahawks won the 2018 and 2014 meetings (27-3 and 30-24). Quote of Note “How aggressive you want to be, based on what their personnel is, what our personnel is, and what gives you the best chance of starting fast. Is it coverage? Is it pressure? Is it a different front? There’s a million variables that go into it. And then what personnel package do we want to start with? What 11 do we want to put out there to start the game, and then have a plan to get to a different one later? So those are all factors. How did we practice that week? What was the best thing that we were executing? ‘All right, I like that as a lead call.’ It’s very interactive, both call-wise and personnel-wise, and it’s a week-long conversation of that back-and-forth decision of what’s best.” —Las Vegas Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard on nuances of starting better defensively

title: Raiders injury news: Trey Zuhn ready to play Sunday

full_text: (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s Week 10 0f the NFL season and most rosters are battered … and then there are the Las Vegas Raiders. The Raiders are in line to have most of their 53 player son their roster healthy and available to play Sunday when they open the Fernando Mendoza era by hosting the Seattle Seahawks at Allegiant Stadium. Kickoff is set for 1:05 p.m. PT. Las Vegas head coach Klint Kubiak said rookie right guard Trey Zuhn has cleared the concussion protocol and he will start Sunday. Zuhn had to leave the Week 9 loss at San Francisco. He practiced on a limited basis Wednesday and Thursday. However, he was a full go Friday. The third-round pick will be making his third straight start. Kubiak said defensive tackle Thomas Booker and wide receiver Dont’e Thornton are both questionable. There are both reserve players. The Raiders have had a major injury advantage in virtually every game this season and that will continue Sunday. The Seahawks will be without starting quarterback Sam Darnold as backup Drew Lock will play. Standout left guard Quenton Nelson and left tackle Charles Cross are out as well as standout defensive tackle Leonard Williams. Kubiak also sad the Raiders are considering adding a third quarterback to the roster behind Mendoza and Aidan O’Connell..

full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here is a look at how the Las Vegas Raiders’ 2024 draft class fared in a 38-17 loss at the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday and what to look for Sunday at home against the Seattle Seahawks. Brock Bowers: The first-round pick played all 50 of the Raiders’ offensive snaps and he had seven catches for 111 yards and a touchdown on eight targets. He had three catches of 20 plus yards and he leads all tight ends with 11 of those plays despite missing two games. What a special, special player. Jackson Powers-Johnson: The second-round pick remained on the bench for the fourth straight game. He played three snaps on special teams. What a fall. D.J. Glaze: The third-round pick started at right tackle as usual. Tommy Eichenberg: The fifth-round pick from Ohio State played 41 percent of the defensive snaps. His role on defense has increased the past three weeks. He had seven tackles for the second time in three games. He also played 18 plays on special teams. He’s a part of things these days. Dylan Laube: The sixth-round pick made a huge impact with a 54-yard kick return against the 49ers. That came a week after he had a 95-yard kick return for a touchdown at the Jets, which earned him the AFC Special Teams Player of the Week award. Laube had 7 returns for 197 yards, for an average of 28.1 yards per return, against the 49ers. He is averaging 32.3 yards per kick return. That leads the league.

summary: The 4-5 Las Vegas Raiders host the 5-4 Seattle Seahawks on Sunday. Kickoff is set for 1:05 p.m. PT. Here are five keys to victory: Be perfect on offense: The Raiders committed five turnovers in the second half of a 38-17 road loss at the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday. The turnovers included two in […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Olszewski/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 4-5 Las Vegas Raiders host the 5-4 Seattle Seahawks on Sunday. Kickoff is set for 1:05 p.m. PT. Here are five keys to victory: Be perfect on offense: The Raiders committed five turnovers in the second half of a 38-17 road loss at the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday. The turnovers included two in the 49ers’ end zone and a Pick Six. That’s not going to work against Seattle. The Raiders are going to have to play clean in Fernando Mendoza’s start debut against that defense to have a chance. Get to the quarterback: Drew Lock is a game manager. The backup, who is playing for an injured Sam Darnold, is not going to wow anyone and he can be forced into making errors. The Raiders must harass him. Use intel: Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak was Seattle’s offensive coordinator last year when they won the Super Bowl. He knows this roster well. He needs to scheme up a win. Brock, Brock, Brock: The Raiders need to be carried by their best player in this game. The tight end is putting up huge numbers every week. Las Vegas has to be willed to victory by Bowers. Fernando find Brock and do it often. Stop the run: Las Vegas has been getting gutted by the run every week. San Francisco had 190 yards on the ground this week. Expect Seattle to try to do the same. Las Vegas has to finally stop the bleeding on the ground.

title: Miami Dolphins Vs. Indianapolis Colts: Three Reasons Why
summary: The 2026 Dolphins have had a tough schedule thus far.  They have only faced 2 teams that currently aren’t in the playoff picture.  One was week 1 against the Raiders when this young team was still wet behind their ears.  The other was a win against their division rival Jets.  They had a lead at […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 4: Kyle McCord #14 of the Miami Dolphins warms up before the game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2026 Dolphins have had a tough schedule thus far. They have only faced 2 teams that currently aren’t in the playoff picture. One was week 1 against the Raiders when this young team was still wet behind their ears. The other was a win against their division rival Jets. They had a lead at halftime against the Pats and kept the most explosive offense in the league in check against the Lions. That schedule is a tough row to hoe but now gets a bit of a reprieve as they face a team that is actually tanking in the Indianapolis Colts. Nothing will be easy though, as we will see later. 3 REASONS THE DOLPHINS CAN WIN THE COLTS OFFENSE IS BAD The Dolphins have been offensively challenged all season with a regressing OL, rookie WRs, an inexperienced QB that is now on IR, and the loss of their most dynamic threat in De’Von Achane. That’s a recipe for bad offensive football and for the first few games, it was. Despite a blip last week against Detroit, they had started to turn things around offensively. The Colts? They have no such excuses. They have one of the best RBs in football with Jonathan Taylor and added pieces like Keenan Allen this offseason to help the receiving unit. None of it has helped and now they have traded away some of the best weapons they had available. Both Allen and WR Josh Downs were traded at the deadline. The WRs left on the active roster are Deion Burks, Ashton Dulin, Anthony Gould, Laquon Treadwell, and former Dolphin Nick Westbrook-Ikhine. They still have TE Tyler Warren and the Dolphins have struggled with covering opposing TEs since… forever. But Warren has cooled off from a hot start to his rookie season. This year, he has only eclipsed 55 yards once and hasn’t found the end zone since week 2. Overall, the Colts average 4.5 yards per play, which is 2nd worst in the league. Taylor is still producing with 161 carries, 656 yards, and 8 rushing TDs. The Colts as a team are 10th in the league is rushing yards with 1037 yards and tied for 4th in rushing TDs with 11. But that is their entire offense. QB Daniel Jones is struggling with barely a 60% CP and a miserable 5.7 YPA. That YPA is tied for worst in the league. They have 6 passing TDs, tied with Miami and some others for league lowest. The Dolphins have faced 5 of the top 10 passing offenses in terms of completion percentage, 4 of them in the top 5. Only the Vikings are in the lower half. After the Dolphins kept a very good Detroit passing offense under 70%, they can absolutely keep up the momentum against a team that isn’t throwing the ball well at all. They may allow some underneath completions as Indy has been throwing short. This is not a scary pass offense at all and with the dearth of WR talent on the roster, Miami’s defense can focus on Taylor and Warren. THE COLTS DEFENSE IS EQUALLY BAD In every game this season, the Dolphins have faced a good overall team, a team with a weaker defense but a dominant offense, or a weaker offense with a dominant defense. This week, the Dolphins get none of the above. The Colts defense is bad across the board in most metrics. They are tied for last in yards per play allowed with 6.1. They allow 362 yards per game. While there isn’t a ranking for that stat specifically, the Dolphins have allowed 326 yards per game for a comparison. Their pass defense is middle of the pack in terms of yards per game allowed at 224.8. Only the Dolphins and Cardinals allow a worst passer rating against than Indy. They are tied with Miami for 2nd worst in YPA allowed. They are solid in CP allowed at 61.4% and are tied for 9th in terms of passes defensed with 44. But they are 2nd to last in INTs with 2 – only the Jets have fewer. They have 19 sacks on the season, but 4 of those belong to DeForest Buckner, who is now in San Fran. They are just below Miami in pressure percentage at 21.8%. In run defense, only the Raiders and Cowboys allow more yards per game than Indy, and only those teams plus the Bengals allow a higher YPC average. The Dolphins offense struggled against a supposed Lions team, but that defense has started to come together. Plus, they have a dangerous pass rush and have been good against the run. The Colts have none of that. The Dolphins and their run-early-and-often offense should have plenty of opportunities to be effective on the ground. THE DOLPHINS DEFENSE JUST MAY HAVE TURNED A CORNER Before the season, I read a tweet that stated Miami would probably have an adjustment period to the defense before it all started to click. Many times, that can take half the season. Half the season in and, lo and behold, the Dolphins defense had their best game of the season. The Lions offense is dangerous, but the Dolphins limited them to nearly 100 yards and 10 points off their season averages. The pass defense played as well as expected against their weaponry and the run defense, which had been faltering, stepped back up against arguably the league’s best RB. The pass rush, which was invisible early in the season, has stepped up in recent games with 25 pressures of their season total of 54 coming in the last 3 games. The stage is set for the Dolphins defense to have their signature game and show the development we’ve all been seeing. Unfortunately for them, they lost stalwart DT Zach Sieler for the season. However, sophomore Kenneth Grant has been stepping it up since his return from IR. He played his arguably best game of the season against the Lions and now will be forced to become a bigger part of the DL equation. The good news is the Colts have traded All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson, and his replacement is rookie Jalen Farmer. The loss of Sieler will sting more in future games, but the stage is set for Grant and the others to have a solid, if not great, game. 3 REASONS THE DOLPHINS COULD LOSE ON THE ROAD AGAIN The Dolphins have not been a team that travels well this season. I mean, they are 1-7, so there aren’t a lot of positives to draw from overall. Now, there are some caveats to this. The 1st 2 games were on the road, and everyone was still in the learning process. One of those teams is the best NFC team. They went back on the road in week 4 to face the league’s best defense. That can skew the stats and make things seem worse than what they are now. They did get their only win of the season on the road against the Jets. That said, we know the offense will be limited now. The defense may have turned a corner, but they allowed the inept Vikings offense to produce 336 yards, which is their 2nd best output this season. They allowed the Jets to have their 2nd best output of the season. The fact is that we really don’t know if the Dolphins have truly grown and developed enough that they can go on the road and play at the levels we hope to see. The Colts, despite their issues, still have a couple dangerous playmakers on both sides of the ball. The Dolphins need to prove it first. SPECIAL TEAMS, PENALTIES, AND THE MARGINS The Dolphins are 31st in average starting field position, starting at their own 28.2. They are 2nd worst in starting field position allowed, allowing opponents to start at their own 36.7. That’s nearly an entire set of downs worth of field position on average. The Dolphins have 13 touchbacks on kickoffs, most in the league and a touchback percentage of 41.9%, the highest in the league. The next highest is 27.5%. The Dolphins have committed 71 penalties thus far , with 9 of them having been declined and 1 offsetting. 33 of those are offensive penalties. They have committed 9 false starts, tied for 9th fewest, but committed 19 holding penalties, 3rd most. Of the 71 penalties called, 19 of them came on 3rd down and 5 were on 4th down. That is basically 1 out of every 3 penalties called. They have 2…

After that last game, if they had asked KOC about the offense’s execution, he should have said (like John McKay may or may not have said) “I’m in favor of it”! Some other McKay one liners … On the Struggling Buccaneers On winless streaks and performance: After an 0–26 start, he joked, “Three or four plane crashes and we’re in the playoffs”, and lamented, “We didn’t tackle well today, but we made up for it by not blocking”. He also noted they could “Can’t stop the pass or the run, otherwise we’re in great shape” and requested a neutral site because they couldn’t play at home or on the road. On Coaching & Football Philosophy On strategy and players: He famously dismissed football emotion by comparing it to his wife Corky and defended giving O.J. Simpson the ball constantly because “it isn’t very heavy”. Down 17–0 at halftime to Notre Dame, he offered the simple math that “If you don’t score more than 17 points, you’ll lose” (USC rallied to win). On Recruiting & Fan Pressure On family and fans: When recruiting his son J.K. McKay to USC, he noted he had the advantage that he “slept with his mother”, and threatened to pay his way to “Peking” if he chose Stanford over USC. To handle hostile fan bases, he joked that he bought up all the rope in Los Angeles to prevent being hung in effigy. Bum Phillips had some funny quotes too … On Coaching & Football On Job Security & Rivals: Quips included noting that coaches are split into “them that’s fired and them that’s gonna be fired”, and praising Don Shula’s ability to “take his’n and beat your’n and take your’n and beat his’n”. On Team Struggles & Drive: Famously remarked, “The harder we played, the behinder we got”, criticized uncoachable extremes, and vowed that after knocking on the Super Bowl door, “Next year we’re going to kick the son of a bitch in!”. On Life & Himself Self-Deprecation & Humor: Remarked he didn’t mind people thinking he was stupid, just didn’t want to prove it, didn’t mind being called Bum without a “you” in front of it, and joked that he brought his wife on road trips because “she’s too ugly to kiss goodbye”. The Astrodome: Noted that “Mama always said that if it can’t rain on you, you’re indoors” when explaining why he didn’t wear his cowboy hat inside the stadium. … sorry, I digressed. I have seen the “report” that the new Vikings regime is down on Caleb Banks and Norse4life posted a link to the story in a feed. Thanks. I will say that it is interesting and curious at best. Banks missed almost all of his final season at Florida and then broke his foot at the 2026 NFL Combine, which kept him out of OTAs, minicamp, and most of training camp. Judging a 6’6″, 327-pound rookie who missed an entire offseason of conditioning on just about 100 NFL snaps is an overreaction. Also, and more importantly, you have to believe the BFlo had significant input into the Banks and Golday picks. If someone is going to criticize the Banks pick because he is not doing much yet then they should “man up” and criticize BFlo too. Problem with that is the Vikings have one of the top defensea in the NFL. I believe the team knows exactly what it is doing with both Banks and Golday and are grooming them for their opportunity just like they did with Dallas Turner. One good thing about Cousins this year is … 2026 Situational Splits by Game Score Breaking down Cousins’s 2026 passing numbers across CBS Sports and NFL.com situational logs reveals a sharp contrast in volume and efficiency depending on the scoreboard: Game State : Cmp / Att : Comp % : Yards : Yds / Att : TD : INT : Sacks : Passer Rating Ahead (Leading) : 28 / 52 : 53.8% : 221 : 4.2 : 4 : 2 : 2 : 74.3 Tied : 44 / 68 : 64.7% : 511 : 7.5 : 4 : 1 : 4 : 100.8 Behind (Trailing) : 130 / 195 : 66.7% : 1,608 : 8.2 : 12 : 5 : 5 : 101.8 Total : 202 / 315 : 64.1% : 2,340 : 7.4 : 20 : 8 : 11 : 97.1 While nearly 69% of Cousins’s passing yards (1,608 of 2,340) came while trailing, looking closely at game scripts shows that most of those yards came in competitive, one-score losses rather than true garbage time. True Blowout / Garbage-Time Games: Cousins played in three multi-score losses where late-game soft coverage inflated volume—a 45–17 loss at New England (Week 5), a 35–21 loss to the Rams (Week 7), and a 38–17 loss at San Francisco (Week 9). Even in those blowouts, Cousins threw only 4 total touchdowns against 3 interceptions, meaning garbage time did not heavily pad his touchdown totals. Conservative Play-Calling While Leading: Cousins attempted just 52 passes all season while ahead, averaging only 4.2 yards per attempt. When Las Vegas held a lead—such as in their 27–13 win over Miami and 26–14 win over the Chargers—the offense leaned heavily on short, ball-control throws and the run game. When ahead by 1 to 8 points specifically, he was sharp in the red zone, throwing 4 touchdowns with 0 interceptions (100.8 passer rating). Strong Performance in Neutral / Close Scripts: In tied game states (68 attempts) and within the 4th quarter of one-score games (±7 points), Cousins maintained a 100.8 and 108.8 passer rating respectively, confirming that his efficiency held up in high-leverage moments. … This is very comforting and confirms the way he played his first go round with KOC. Cousins tied the NFL single-season record with 8 fourth-quarter comebacks and 8 game-winning drives during his first season with head coach Kevin O’Connell in 2022. The stats above prove that he plays best when the game is close or his team is behind. You like that! We got Kirk,’ ” Addison explained this week a few lockers down from the one that now has Cousins’ No. 8 jersey. “I was like, ‘Wow, Kirko Chainz is really back. It’s like 2023 all over again.’ “ … Familiarity with the coaching staff and multiple teammates have helped Cousins reacclimate to the Vikings locker room this week. “I cannot give him enough credit for coming in here, how he’s going about the week, both him and the coaching staff, getting him ready to go, working extremely hard, using all the time we possibly can,” O’Connell said. “It’s been really impressive what he’s been able to do and just the command and just getting right back in the huddle with a lot of guys he’s played with, but certainly some guys he hasn’t. And it’s been something that everybody’s been very, very impressed by.” Addison sizzled in his time with Cousins — he caught 36 passes for 482 yards and seven touchdowns in his first eight pro games — but the sample size was shortened when Cousins suffered the injury in Week 8 of 2023 at Lambeau Field. “I was super excited to get a guy of his caliber, and he’s familiar with the offense. He’s been around these weapons. Hopefully we get back on the same page, right where we left off,” said Addison, who was then asked to summarize Thursday’s practice and said, “It felt like he never left. The chemistry is still there.” … Jefferson, who launched his career at a prolific pace by snagging passes from Cousins from 2020-23, said “it’s definitely exciting to have a guy like him back in the building.” “We know how he…

title: SB Nation Reacts Results: Yes, We Do Like That!
summary: It’s a little earlier than we usually get them to you, but we’ve got our SB Nation Reacts results for this week about our Minnesota Vikings, and we’ve even got some bonus results for you this week! So, let’s go ahead and get to those here. Our first question for this week was, as always, […]
full_text: EAGAN, MN - NOVEMBER 11, 2026: Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins addresses the media during a press conference at the TCO Performance Center in Eagan, Minn., on Sunday, Nov. 11, 2026. (Photo by Elizabeth Flores/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images) It’s a little earlier than we usually get them to you, but we’ve got our SB Nation Reacts results for this week about our Minnesota Vikings, and we’ve even got some bonus results for you this week! So, let’s go ahead and get to those here. Our first question for this week was, as always, how you feel about the direction of the team. And if we had started and ended the survey on Monday night, the returns may have found a way to dip into the negative numbers. However, shortly after the Monday Night debacle against Buffalo, the Vikings pulled the trigger on a big trade. . .we’ll get to that in a bit. . .and that shifted things upward a bit. With this being the midway point of the season, our graphics folks put together a look at how our confidence figures have gone this season, along with key points along the way. As you can see, despite the Vikings being the last undefeated team in the NFL, the ol’ confidence graph has been pretty up-and-down over the course of the season so far, due largely to the struggles of the offense. This week, we’re back up above 50%. . .not by much, but we’re still there. . .and, hopefully, we can get that number even higher this next week. Which brings us to our other question for this week, which was us asking you to grade the deal the Vikings made for Kirk Cousins with the Las Vegas Raiders. The Vikings wound up trading a 2027 third-round pick. . .the (much) lower of the two third-rounders they currently possess. . .to acquire Cousins’ services for the rest of the season, and they needed to do something after what we saw from the quarterback position over the first half of this season. So, what did people think? Well, we got a majority on this one, with 59% of those who responded to our poll giving the deal a solid “A” grade. Another 29% gave the deal a B, so a full 88%. . .isn’t that a convenient number. . .think this is an above average deal for our favorite team. Another 8% gave it a “C” grade, while the other 4% of those who responded were evenly split between “D” and “F” grades for the deal. Honestly. . .for a third-round pick, there is just about no downside to this deal for the Vikings. Cousins doesn’t have to be great for this team to be successful. He just has to be. . .you know. . . not what Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz have been this season. Then, maybe the Vikings’ defense won’t have to be on the field for 40 minutes a game and they can crush opposing offenses in the fourth quarter just as badly as they crush them in the first two or three quarters. It isn’t just Vikings fans who like the Cousins trade, either. The folks from the mothership asked which of the trades that happened at or around the trade deadline in the NFL would make the biggest impact and, well. . . . . .the majority of people said it was the Kirk Cousins trade, with 54% of people who responded to their poll declaring that to be the biggest move around the league. The only one that was even close was the Bears acquiring defensive lineman Jeffery Simmons from the Tennessee Titans, which got 35% of the vote. Here’s hoping that will be the way things work out for the Vikings as far as this trade is concerned. Those are our SB Nation Reacts results for this week, ladies and gentlemen. As always, we want to thank all of you who took the time to participate in our polls for this week, and keep your eyes open for next week’s questions! Check out the FanDuel Sportsbook , the official sportsbook partner of SB Nation .

title: A Realistic View of What Kirk Cousins 2.0 Brings to the Vikings
summary: The Minnesota Vikings made the move they had to make after a half-season of underwhelming quarterback performance in trading for Kirk Cousins. He will be the starter as soon as possible, which is likely to be this Sunday against the Packers. His arrival has come with much fanfare as the savior of the Vikings offense […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 23: Kirk Cousins #8 of the Minnesota Vikings throws a pass during an NFL football game between the Minnesota Vikings and the San Francisco 49ers at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 23, 2023 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) The Minnesota Vikings made the move they had to make after a half-season of underwhelming quarterback performance in trading for Kirk Cousins. He will be the starter as soon as possible, which is likely to be this Sunday against the Packers. His arrival has come with much fanfare as the savior of the Vikings offense who, combined with the Vikings dominant defense and good special teams, could position the Vikings for a deep run in the post-season. But a quarterback switching teams in mid-season is not without its difficulties, even with Cousins’ familiarity with Kevin O’Connell’s scheme and some of the key players around him from Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, and T.J. Hockenson to Brian O’Neill, Blake Brandel, and Christian Darrisaw. It’s also an advantage that Cousins has been playing the entire season, so he doesn’t have to get acclimated to playing again, as a backup quarterback who hasn’t played would need to do. Command of the Offense If Cousins plays on Sunday (as expected at this point), there could be some hiccups as he works out timing and other rapport issues in his first game back after three years. But Cousins has been playing in the same type of offense under Klint Kubiak in Las Vegas, and is probably the most well-versed quarterback in Kevin O’Connell’s scheme in the league- and one of the most well-suited to execute it. The first graphic compares Cousins’ rate and EPA efficiency in the play-action passing game, which is central to KOC’s offense. He’s been one of the more effective quarterbacks out of play-action for most of his career, and has run it at a relatively high rate for most of his 15-year career. He’s also played at a relatively high rate from under center, which KOC also likes to do to make the play-action game more effective. Cousins’ career passer rating from under center is 107.2, and in play-action it is 110.0. This season, Cousins’ passer rating with play-action is 123.4. The Vikings have used play-action more than the Raiders have so far this season. Part of that is game situation- both down-and-distance and score/time remaining. You would think that with the Vikings dominant defense, they would continue to be able to run play action at a high rate to maximize Cousins’ strength in that area. The second graphic represents Cousins’ passing metrics to each part of the field. The big takeaway is that the lion’s share of Cousins’ passing yards and attempts are between the numbers. He’s also had good success throwing at intermediate depth (10-19 yards) this season. That’s another important element of KOC’s scheme-targeting the middle of the field. Both Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz have been reluctant to target the middle of the field, which compromises the effectiveness of O’Connell’s scheme. One of the staples of O’Connell’s scheme is the dagger route combination, which has largely disappeared from run or targeted routes this season. It’s also one of the most effective route combinations for Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison. Bottom line, having Kirk Cousins at quarterback should open up the entirety of KOC’s playbook, but it may take some time for Cousins to re-familiarize himself with the playbook and get on the same page again with receivers. Still, I don’t anticipate Cousins hesitating to get the ball out to open receivers as Murray and Wentz have done this season. Differences Between Kirk 1.0 and Kirk 2.0 and Murray and Wentz Since the last time Cousins played for the Vikings- three years ago- he had his Achilles tendon repaired and spent most of his time in Atlanta recovering from that. At that point it looked like he was done. His passes lacked velocity and his movement was slower than it had been. Apparently, he couldn’t really push off of his foot with the repaired Achilles and that was negatively affecting his game. But after signing with the Raiders, it appears that Cousins has fully recovered from the Achilles injury and no longer has the issues that plagued him in Atlanta. The velocity is back and while Cousins has never been particularly mobile, he is able to move like he used to before the Achilles injury. According to Albert Breer, when the Vikings were looking into trading for Cousins, after, “meshing the scouts’ and coaches’ analysis, they saw Cousins as still possessing a live arm and deadly accuracy and having returned to the baseline of athleticism he set before tearing his Achilles in 2024, evidenced on tape in the keeper game that’s essential to Kubiak’s scheme.” I’ve watched all of Cousins’ throws with the Raiders this year, and it is reminiscent of his previous stint with the Vikings. I don’t know that his arm strength has declined much- it doesn’t look like it- but there is a caveat. He can make all the throws, as you would expect from a starting NFL quarterback, but he needs to step-in to deeper throws for them to have the needed velocity. That may have been the case before as well but it is something that stood out when watching his tape this season. He can’t launch balls down field with velocity off his back foot like Jordan Love or Caleb Williams. This is the impact of being his being 38 years old. Additionally, he has not become any more mobile over the last three years, and the scampering of Kyler Murray to pick up first downs here and there is definitely not in Cousins’ bag, if that wasn’t obvious. He has run for five-yard gains on a couple occasions this season, but that’s about it. He is able to maneuver within the pocket effectively and does fine on bootlegs, but he’s not going to outrun many pass rushers for very long. He’s also not afraid to deliver the ball downfield in the face of oncoming pressure- and pay the price for it. He’s also not afraid of throwing into tight windows and does so with regularity. Cousins has 8 interceptions so far this season, three of which came last weekend against the 49ers. A few of them came on throws left a bit short, a few in tight window throws where ball placement and/or route were not ideal. One his receiver fell down. And the last one came with 4 minutes left in the 49ers game and he was just trying make something happen down multiple scores. But for the most part Cousins’ interceptions came while being aggressive and playing on time making throws that Murray and Wentz have generally avoided this season. Kirk Cousins 58 YIA here in stride for the touchdown. He's always had a strong, tho not elite arm, and it hasn't declined. pic.twitter.com/qGFOI7iHSv — Jackson McIntire (@2HighCoverage) November 13, 2026 Cousins hasn’t been sacked much so far this season- just 11 times in 9 games. He’s also the only quarterback who has not been sacked on a blitz so far this season. So, he’s generally done an excellent job of avoiding the rush and getting the ball out- maybe only one of sacks can be blamed on him. And whereas Murray or Wentz may look to scramble to buy time, Cousins is mainly focused on getting the ball out. He’s very much a pocket passer in that respect, with his only move typically being to step up in the pocket to avoid the edge rush. The Raiders offense has different strengths than the Vikings, and that has influenced Cousins’ play. Their offensive line is similar strength as the Vikings, anchored by All-Pro center Tyler Linderbaum. But the strength of their receiver group is their tight ends- Brock Bowers and Michael Mayer- and they run double tight-end sets at the highest rate in the league. Their receivers are Tre Tucker and former Viking Jalen Nailor. The Raiders running game is terrible- last in the league- averaging just 2.9 yards per carry. Ashton Jeanty hasn’t done much as a running back, but he is a good receiving back. So, roughly 60% of Cousins’…

title: On Kirk Cousins (and Packers Week, Too!)
summary: Kirk Cousins is once again the quarterback for the Minnesota Vikings. Welcome to the most exciting, if anxiety-riddled, stretch of Vikings football in memory. The next few months will be unlike any other. General manager Nolan Teasley did what he had to do. A 3rd-round pick was a small price to pay to avoid the […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - SEPTEMBER 13: Kirk Cousins #8 of the Minnesota Vikings passes the ball in the second quarter of the game against the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2020 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Kirk Cousins is once again the quarterback for the Minnesota Vikings. Welcome to the most exciting, if anxiety-riddled, stretch of Vikings football in memory. The next few months will be unlike any other. General manager Nolan Teasley did what he had to do. A 3rd-round pick was a small price to pay to avoid the iceberg. After an embarrassing, mind-boggling, inept offensive showing in front of the entire nation on Monday Night Football that threatened a full-on locker room mutiny and the season’s implosion, the ship has now been steered into calmer waters. Whether it will be there when the calendar turns to January is still very much up in the air. The only situations even remotely comparable were Sam Bradford’s arrival days before the 2016 season and Randy Moss’ return in 2010. While the former started well, defeating the Green Bay Packers in Week 1, it ultimately petered out. The latter didn’t even get that far. Let’s hope for better luck this time around. NARRATIVES, NARRATIVES EVERYWHERE! Super Bowl Dreams Are Back On. Through nine games as the Raiders’ starter, with offensive weapons no one would confuse with the 1999 Rams, Kirk Cousins was on pace for more TD passes (38) than he had with the Vikings (2021 and 2022) after the NFL moved to a 17-game regular season. He would just fall short of the passing yardage he had in 2022 (4,547). In an earlier article, I noted that a torn Achilles in a quarterback’s plant leg is the worst non-throwing-arm injury you can sustain. Recovery is challenging and often takes more than one season before you start to look like yourself again. I think that may explain much of what’s going on with Daniel Jones in Indy right now. Given his performance this year, there is a persuasive argument that the nature of the injury, not necessarily age, may explain the inconsistency Cousins experienced during his stint with the Atlanta Falcons. Would he have played better if he were 25? Probably. But his play for the Raiders has been a pleasant surprise that no one envisioned before the season: 2nd in passing TDs, 5th in yards, 9th in EPA per dropback, etc. All Cousins needs to do is be good. That’s it. The Raiders are 8th in points per game (26.4). We won’t even need that 95% of the time. We’d be 8-0 right now. The reason the Silver and Black are 4-5 is that their defense is last in points allowed (29.8) and yards allowed (385.4). They’re basically the 2020-21 Vikings. Under Brian Flores, we’re 1st and 2nd in those categories, respectively. The NFC is wide open right now. No one is convincing me that there is a team we can’t beat, with Cousins back throwing to Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, and T.J. Hockenson again, and Flores’ defense as the ultimate insurance policy. Cousins, Storybook Ending? Hollywood’s most gifted screenwriters couldn’t come up with a better scenario. Cousins returns to the Vikings to save the season, and his first game is at Lambeau Field – the very place his Vikings tenure ended the first time around. All under the larger theme of redemption, given how those highly debated years ended after the 2023 season. Can’t make it up: Vikings play “Higher” by Creed at Kirk Cousins’ first practice back with them. pic.twitter.com/NYLOld9d64 — Kevin Seifert (@SeifertESPN) November 12, 2026 Cousins realizes the feel-good, storybook ending is within reach. Reports say the Raiders left the trade decision in his hands. He knows. This is his last, best chance. A Kirk Cousins with a Super Bowl ring would not only have a legitimate Hall of Fame resume (the numbers will be there), but he’d also have a statue outside U.S. Stadium to immortalize his role in ending the long-suffering anguish of a tortured fan base. Patience is a virtue. I’d urge people not to expect Cousins to come in seamlessly and pick up where he left off in 2023. It may take a game or two to get back into a rhythm with the offense and receivers, regardless of previous experience. That certainly doesn’t mean we won’t win on Sunday. We’ve already beaten the Packers and have won games this season with an offense that made us long for the days of the Wishbone or Single-Wing. This is about ensuring the offense is hitting its stride heading into December and (hopefully) a memorable playoff run. KOC Gets a Mulligan (For Now). Cousins’ return effectively gives KOC a new lease on life after repeatedly stepping on rakes with disastrous quarterback decisions that necessitated the trade. He may have gotten away with the don’t look at me! routine in drafting J.J. McCarthy and letting Sam Darnold walk, but the 2026 quarterback room mess is on him. You can only play that hand so many times. Kwesi Adofo-Mensah took the blame for the earlier missteps and lost his job. Nolan Teasley can justifiably plead ignorance for being late to the game, and no one believes he traded McCarthy without KOC’s approval (or encouragement). Regardless of how this season ends, the Vikings will again begin the offseason back at the drawing board at the most important position on the field. The best-case scenario is that Cousins thrives and reworks his deal to replay the role he played with the Raiders this season if the Vikings try yet again to hit on the QBOTF in the draft. Or maybe they can swing a risky trade for Justin Herbert and effectively blow up their cap as several key in-house free agents loom. Does a Daniel Jones trade happen? Do people think Geno Smith or Mac Jones could be the answer? The bill for the Murray-McCarthy mess will eventually come due. Let’s hope KOC still has the currency to pay it without breaking a sweat. I’ve said before that the best-case scenario and the Vikings often go together like hot fudge and sushi. But we’re due for a break after botching the quarterback situation as badly as possible, only to go back to where we started. Right? Right? Kirk Cousins isn’t coming back in another three years to save us again. Well, we are the Vikings, so you never know. That wouldn’t even crack the Top 20 for the weirdest things to happen to this franchise. OH YEAH, THE PACKERS… With Vikings fans and the Minnesota district manager at Kohl’s basking in the excitement of the Cousins trade and renewed hopes for a Super Bowl run, there is a game to play against the stupid Green Bay Packers. As much as it pains me to say it, the Packers come into this one on a roll. They thoroughly destroyed the New England Patriots on the road last week and have won five of their last six. Vikings on Offense All eyes will be on Kirk Cousins and the Vikings offense. The good news is that as long as Cousins doesn’t miss the team bus, it’ll immediately be an improvement over what we’ve seen recently. Like last season without Micah Parsons, the Packers’ defense is good, if not quite elite. He’s close to returning but won’t play in this one. They’re 11th in both points and total yards allowed, but better (Top 5) in yards per play and defensive DVOA. Pass defense is their strength, as they’re in the Top 10 in both pass EPA allowed and passer rating allowed. The Packers have also feasted on interceptions and are 2nd in the NFL. Their run defense looks to be middle of the pack across most traditional and advanced metrics. Hopefully this can be exploited early to get Cousins comfortable and open up the play-action pass game he excelled at under KOC the first time around. I’m genuinely curious how much of the playbook will be open to Cousins with such a short prep, regardless of familiarity. KOC may have commented on this, but if he did, I missed it. As I noted above, however, it may be too much to expect him to just drop in and play as if he never left. Give it some time. What matters is how this offense looks heading into…

full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 29: Josh Jacobs #8 of the Green Bay Packers runs with the ball during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game against the Carolina Panthers at Lambeau Field on October 29, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. LP = Limited participant in practice. DNP = Did not participate in practice. NIR = Not injury related. PUP = Physically unable to participate list. IR = Injured reserve. Note: only starters on IR are listed. Player Name* = Starter. Injury designation definitions: Probable = the league defines a Probable injury designation as a 75% or greater chance of playing. Historically, 95% of players designated probable are active and played on game day. Questionable = the league defines a Questionable injury designation as being ‘uncertain’ of whether the player will play or not. This replaces the former definition of having a 50% chance of playing. Historically, 70-75% of players with a Questionable injury designation were active and played on game day. Doubtful = The league defines a Doubtful injury designation to mean the player is unlikely to participate in the game. In practical terms, teams use the designation when a player has less than a 50% chance to suit up, and active game appearances from this designation remain rare. Historically only around 6% of players with a Doubtful designation are active and played on game day. Out = will not play. Players with this designation are not active on game day and league rules prohibit them from playing. Notes on Injured Players For the Vikings, kind of the worst-case scenario based on the injury list earlier this week, with only Kyle Van Noy being upgraded today among previous DNP players- the rest of which are out on Sunday, including Blake Cashman, T.J. Hockenson, Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins, Jauan Jennings, and Kyler Murray. Moreover, Jordan Addison and Josh Metellus were added to the injury report as both were limited on Friday and carry questionable injury designations. Hopefully both will be able to go on Sunday, however. Not having Hockenson will make it a bit tougher for the debut of Kirk Cousins on Sunday while not having Blake Cashman means Eric Wilson may have the green dot on defense on Sunday with a greater role for Ivan Pace Jr. and probably Jake Golday as well. For the Packers, starters Josh Jacobs, Sean Rhyan, and Micah Parsons are out, as expected. Starting linebacker Zaire Franklin is doubtful, meaning he probably won’t play on Sunday. A few other starters are questionable for the Packers on Sunday, including right guard Kevin Zeitler, defensive end Lukas Van Ness, and safeties Javon Bullard and Xavier McKinney- who was added to the injury list on Friday with a foot injury. Lastly, running back Chris Brooks is also questionable, and with Josh Jacobs out on Sunday may be expected to have more of a role if he’s able to go. But while I expect most of the questionable players to play on Sunday for the Packers, most of them have injuries that may keep them at less than 100%. Overall, both teams are a bit banged up and will be missing some key starters on Sunday. Follow me on X/Bluesky @wludford

summary: Kirk Cousins can help the Vikings beat the Packers—but can Minnesota survive his mistakes? full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 29: Kirk Cousins #8 of the Minnesota Vikings talks with head coach Kevin O'Connell during the third quarter against the Minnesota Vikings at Lambeau Field on October 29, 2023 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images Kirk Cousins can help the Vikings beat the Packers—but can Minnesota survive his mistakes? On this episode of The Real Forno Show , Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano break down a rivalry matchup defined by quarterback decisions, explosive plays, and defensive pressure. The Vikings 1st & SKOL discussion centers on whether Cousins can revive Minnesota’s passing attack while Brian Flores finds ways to disrupt Jordan Love. Forness frames the challenge simply: “Well, it’s gonna boil down to two things: Kirk Cousins and Jordan Love.” For Vikings fans, that means balancing optimism about a more productive offense with realistic expectations about turnovers. Cousins’ biggest opportunity is restoring timing and confidence over the middle, particularly with Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, and T.J. Hockenson. Stefano highlights the appeal: “Now, what I like about Kirk Cousins is he’s not afraid to throw over the middle.” Forness also explains how Cousins’ consistent drop depth could help Christian Darrisaw and Brian O’Neill anticipate where their quarterback will be. However, that structure comes with less mobility than Minnesota had with Kyler Murray. According to the episode’s data, Cousins has taken sacks on just 9.2% of his pressures, but avoiding sacks does not always mean making safe throws. Forness warns, “You’re gonna see Kirk do a Kirk thing, and it’s going to drive you nuts.” The hosts also discuss whether age and accumulated throwing volume could affect his effectiveness later in the season. Key takeaways from the episode Attack the middle: Cousins’ anticipation could help Jefferson, Addison, and Hockenson turn open windows into sustained drives. Expect a protection adjustment: Cousins offers predictable pocket positioning, but opponents can pressure him differently because he lacks Murray’s escapability. Make Love uncomfortable: Forness identifies pressure as essential to limiting Green Bay’s explosive passing attack. Watch the linebacker matchup: With Blake Cashman expected to miss the game, Ivan Pace Jr.’s coverage and decision-making become major storylines alongside Eric Wilson. Respect Green Bay’s receiving threats: Matthew Golden, Christian Watson, and Tucker Kraft give Love opportunities to punish defensive breakdowns. Avoid forcing throws: Evan Williams and Xavier McKinney make manipulating the Packers’ safeties a priority. Follow the coaching counters: Matt LaFleur’s adjustments against Flores could determine which team controls the game. Listen: View Link Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: Green Bay’s struggling offensive line does not make this an easy assignment. Forness argues that Love’s ability to generate explosive completions can overcome inconsistent down-to-down offense, especially if Minnesota gives him time to find receivers. Meanwhile, Cousins must turn possessions into points without feeding an opportunistic Packers secondary. Stefano captures the offensive standard: “Just as long as he’s scoring touchdowns and keeping drives alive, I’ll be happy.” Watch or listen to The Real Forno Show with Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano, a Minnesota Vikings podcast from Vikings 1st & SKOL, for the full quarterback breakdown and rivalry preview. Fan with Us!!! Tyler Forness @TheRealForno of Vikings 1st & SKOL @Vikings1stSKOL and A to Z Sports @AtoZSportsNFL , with Dave Stefano @Luft_Krigare producing this Vikings 1st & SKOL production, the @RealFornoShow found at the @BleavNetwork . So here’s the question, Vikings fans: Which matters more to a Vikings victory: Cousins sustaining drives or Flores shutting down Love’s explosive plays? Or Both?

title: 3-Point Stance: Defense could be a roadblock in Patriots’ playoff pursuit
summary: Last week, I wrote that the New England Patriots shouldn’t preemptively deal an impact player at the NFL trade deadline amid defensive players Christian Barmore and Carlton Davis reportedly being available for trade. Ultimately, the Patriots didn’t make any transactions on Tuesday. Although I cited the offseason as a better time to move either defender, […]
full_text: Last week, I wrote that the New England Patriots shouldn’t preemptively deal an impact player at the NFL trade deadline amid defensive players Christian Barmore and Carlton Davis reportedly being available for trade . Ultimately, the Patriots didn’t make any transactions on Tuesday. Although I cited the offseason as a better time to move either defender, I noted the defense’s encouraging Week Eight performance against the now 1-7 Miami Dolphins as a potential turning point for what has largely been an underwhelming and injured unit through the first half of the season. That didn’t stick. It’s hard not to be concerned about New England’s defense after last Sunday’s deflating performance against the Green Bay Packers. Those reservations are especially warranted when the Patriots’ most expensive cornerback room in the league allows two receivers, Matthew Golden and Christian Watson, to combine for 335 yards and two touchdowns, with each logging career highs. All-Pro Christian Gonzalez, entering 2026 on a four-year, $135 million contract extension, allowed 10 receptions for 187 yards, per NextGen Stats. “I’m a Christian Gonzalez fan,” NFL Hall of Famer Ty Law said on WEEI’s The Greg Hill Show . “I just expect more out of him … I have never been a part of a situation in my 15-year career where a secondary played that bad … That’s unacceptable … You got the bag. You have to play better. “I’m seeing a lot of things that aren’t right when it comes to the New England Patriots’ secondary. Where is the leadership? Where is the communication? … Is it the players or the coaching?” After the game, Gonzalez took responsibility for his poor performance but also isn’t “too worried about it.” “I think Christian [Gonzalez] just did it to himself,” two-time Super Bowl champion Logan Ryan said on the Up & Adams Show . “I loved his comment … He said, ‘Hey, I’m allowed to have a bad day. I had a bad day.’ He doesn’t have a lot of them, and that’s going to happen. Watson and Golden are different [types of receivers] … He had to deal with them both. “Part of being a number one corner is that you have to guard whatever comes out there … Credit to what Green Bay did, but I think mentally he was in his head. He had a slow start, and [then] it continued … That’s the life of being a number one cornerback. You have to bounce back, and I think he will.” Head coach Mike Vrabel acknowledged that he expects more from Gonzalez while emphasizing that the rest of the defense must improve overall. Gonzalez’s struggles are surprising, but the organization paid him for a reason. Another performance like that would be an outlier. Still, his shortcomings highlight an underlying factor that has seen a steady decline in not only Gonzalez’s play but also the inconsistencies of the defense. A lack of execution Over the past week, Patriots defenders across multiple positional groups have cited execution as something to improve upon. Veteran safety Kevin Byard frequently alluded to that sentiment when discussing the Packers’ explosive plays. “We just didn’t execute enough,” Byard said on Sunday. “We knew that was going to be the key to the game, eliminating the big play, and we didn’t do good enough today at all. We all have to be better.” Linebacker and captain Robert Spillane emphasized a similar message Wednesday on The Greg Hill Show , stressing the importance of playing complementary football ahead of Sunday’s matchup against the Detroit Lions, whose offense shares similarities with Green Bay’s. “You put pressure on [Jared Goff] by stopping the run early, by forcing third-and-long passing situations, by being up on the scoreboard, by starting fast as a team, as a unit, and that’s all three phases. I think it’s really a collection of how we play as a team to get that done.” What does that execution come down to? It encompasses everything the team prepares for. Against the Packers, it was schematic and assignment breakdowns. Against the Chicago Bears in Week Seven, it was a lack of physicality. The defense allowed Chicago to notch 30 points on the evening and score on six of its nine offensive drives. Poor tackling plagued the unit throughout the game, giving up 161 yards after the catch. Vrabel’s defense appeared a step behind, exemplifying symptoms of a Super Bowl hangover. Following Sunday night’s loss, outside questions emerged about whether the lack of execution stems from a downward shift in team culture and energy nine months removed from the franchise’s championship appearance. When speaking with reporters in the locker room, wide receiver Mack Hollins said that players content with New England’s performance are “probably not meant for this team,” while DeMario Douglas called for more energy and support from each unit on the sideline. Vrabel echoed the need for better execution on Monday, specifically addressing Gonzalez’s lackluster performance, explaining that “you can’t take a nap in this league.” “You just can’t take a play off or think that they’re not going to challenge or throw the ball at you,” he said. “That’s it. You can’t think that you’re going to not draw attention.” Vrabel, however, views it as a preparation issue, seeing Hollins’ view and his comments about wanting players who want to be with the team as a reminder of the standards required to build the program he envisions. “Whatever reps we get, we have to make them count,” Vrabel said. ”We have to understand, if it’s a jog through, how we show the details of the play and make sure that we understand that.“ Regardless of the state of the team’s culture, poor execution and a lack of physicality are capping a defense that was slated to build on last season’s performance, ranking No. 4 in scoring defense. Healthier defense, underperforming results Statistically, the defense has played better while dealing with injuries compared to finally fielding a healthy starting group. Over the last three games, New England is giving up an average of 31.3 points per game, an increase from 18.8 through the first six contests. Squaring off with the Dolphins in Miami, things were trending upward as the divisional foes managed only five first downs in 10 offensive series. For reference, the game marked the first time the starting cornerback trio of Gonzalez, Carlton Davis and Marcus Jones all played together since Week Three. While Davis is ruled out for Sunday with a knee injury, the defense is still nearly whole. So far this season, the defense ranks 31st against under-center snaps and 32nd when facing early-down play-action. Their corrections against a Lions offense that frequently operates under center and has plenty of success running one of the highest play-action rates in the league. Offense hampered by injuries With so many injuries, the Patriots’ offense hasn’t established a rhythm all season. They simply haven’t had the pieces. Although A.J. Brown, Rhamondre Stevenson and Reggie Gilliam were limited in practice this week, New England only recently welcomed Mack Hollins back to the lineup. The Patriots also remain without Alijah Vera-Tucker, Romeo Doubs, TreVeyon Henderson and Mike Onwenu (potentially sidelined for the season), each potentially sidelined for the season, while Hunter Henry continues to play banged up. Even if a select few of those names return against Detroit, the defense needs to elevate its play to help New England get back in the win column consistently by keeping the offense in scoring range. The Patriots are still 5-4 and in the playoff picture, but with a tough rest-of-season schedule and the Houston Texans sneaking into the playoff bubble, things need to turn around swiftly.
author: Andrew Guindon

title: 5 questions and answers about Patriots vs. Lions
summary: The New England Patriots are taking on an unfamiliar opponent in an unfamiliar location this week. Playing its first ever game in the German city of Munich, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel will face a Detroit Lions squad it hasn’t gone up against since 2022 — three years prior to Vrabel’s arrival. So, […]
full_text: The New England Patriots are taking on an unfamiliar opponent in an unfamiliar location this week. Playing its first ever game in the German city of Munich, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel will face a Detroit Lions squad it hasn’t gone up against since 2022 — three years prior to Vrabel’s arrival. So, to find out more about the Lions, we spoke with Ryan Mathews of Pats Pulpit’s sister site Pride of Detroit , the SB Nation community for all things Lions. 1. The Lions have been one of the least efficient coverage teams in the league, but their pass rush has been ferocious. Do you think Detroit’s pass rush is enough to keep Drake Maye from playing more like he did in October than he did last week? To answer that, we need to adjust one premise ever so slightly: Detroit’s pass rush is more very good than dominant, and its back-end coverage is still where Lions fans want to believe in the progress that’s been made over the past four games. The Lions sit seventh in the NFL in both pressure rate (41.2% of 354 dropbacks) and sacks (27), yet opposing offenses are still averaging 0.143 EPA per dropback against them—the fourth-worst mark in the league. However, over the last four games, the Lions are averaging 0.016 EPA per dropback, which has them ranked 20th — improvement! Drake Maye is going to be their biggest test since Jordan Love came to Ford Field in Week 7. Love thrives on pushing the ball down the field to create big plays, and Detroit’s defense did a commendable job keeping him in check, relatively speaking. He had 10 deep pass attempts, the most among quarterbacks in Week 7, and his average depth of target was 10.9 yards, but his yards per attempt (6.09) ranked 21st and his pass success rate ranked 26th. Detroit’s defense pressured Love on 17 of his dropbacks in that game, and that played a key role in putting a lid on the deep-passing attack, so they’re going to need to keep the pressure on Maye to get similar results from their secondary. 2. The Lions have one of the deepest groups of skill players in the NFL. Has anyone managed to slow this group down, and if so, how? And would playing man coverage against them be foolish? Detroit’s skill position players do run deep. Be it Jameson Williams’ speed, Amon-Ra St. Brown or Sam LaPorta’s craftiness in their route running and understanding of zone coverage, or Jahmyr Gibbs’ ability to do it all, they have plenty of ways to test opposing defenses. Interestingly enough, Jared Goff ranks fourth out of 33 qualifying quarterbacks in EPA/dropback both against zone (0.194) and man (0.304) coverage — granted he’s only registered 29 dropbacks against man coverage per SumerSports — so it’s going to be interesting to see if New England sticks to their guns and plays as much man as they normally do. 3. Jahmyr Gibbs’ speed is the headliner when discussing the talented running back, but what else has allowed the Lions’ ground game to be so successful? Gibbs’ speed doesn’t show up directly in the box score, but the underlying rushing metrics point to his contact balance and elusiveness as major drivers of Detroit’s ground attack. Across 177 carries for 847 yards (4.79 yards per carry) and nine touchdowns, Gibbs has forced 53 missed tackles (first in the NFL) and averages 3.33 yards after contact (t-12th). The explosive-play upside, generating 36.1% of his rushing yardage on carries of 12 or more yards. Backup Sione Vaki has come on as of late, offering solid physicality as a runner and a pass protector–albeit in limited action— averaging 4.5 yards per carry and 3.53 yards after contact across just 30 carries. Schematically, Detroit leans heavily on outside zone, which accounts for 98 designed runs (excluding QB scrambles and kneels) at 4.92 yards per carry, but the offensive line has been inconsistent in their run blocking: the Lions rank 25th in stuffed rate, and it feels like the majority of that is on the big guys up front. Inside zone has actually been Detroit’s most efficient concept at 5.35 yards per carry and 0.156 EPA, largely because defenses can rarely afford to load the box against the Lions. Detroit’s facing eight or more defenders on just 15% of its 20 carries, compared to 40.8% for outside zone. Gap concepts like power and counter have struggled in small samples: ten carries for each concept, averaging 3.3 to 3.4 yards respectively. 4. Who are some underrated Lions playmakers who Patriots fans should know ahead of this game? Looking strictly at skill-position production behind top headliners Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jahmyr Gibbs, there are three names that consistently pull their weight without always getting the national headlines. Jameson Williams often gets typecast as a vertical threat, but he’s at his best when he’s catching passes through holes in zone coverage and making defenses pay with his speed after the catch. His elusiveness is a really underrated aspect of his game. Williams has turned 46 targets into 28 catches for 468 yards and five touchdowns so far this season, posting a strong 16.7 yards per catch — 21st in the NFL. Sam LaPorta is a reliable chain-mover over the middle, but his usage has dwindled in recent weeks ever since he publicly commented on his contract situation. Not saying, but I’m saying, you know. But maybe the most overlooked player in the Lions offense as of late is the aforementioned Sione Vaki. He’s settling well into a complementary role behind Gibbs, earning the trust of the coaching staff to the point where there have been whole series as of late where Gibbs scantily sees the field. 5. The Lions are seen as 2.5-point favorites for this weekend’s matchup. What happened if the Patriots pull off an upset? What happened if they lost their second game in a row? The Patriots will have pulled off the upset if their offensive line provides enough protection for Maye to air it out for big explosive plays. On defense, if they stop the Lions’ run game and force them to operate from behind the sticks in the passing game, it’s highly likely New England will leave Germany with a victory. Detroit gets the win if they pressure Maye relentlessly and he continues to turn the ball over, setting up the Lions offense with short fields to put points on the board.

title: Milton Williams takes action to address Patriots’ penalty problem
summary: Pre-snap penalties have been a major problem for the New England Patriots defense this season.  Defensive tackle Milton Williams has had enough. “I put in fines this week,” the defensive tackle revealed Friday “$1,000 fine for whoever jumps offsides.” Williams has been guilty of the infraction himself, getting flagged twice in the first three weeks […]
full_text: Pre-snap penalties have been a major problem for the New England Patriots defense this season. Defensive tackle Milton Williams has had enough. “I put in fines this week,” the defensive tackle revealed Friday “$1,000 fine for whoever jumps offsides.” Williams has been guilty of the infraction himself, getting flagged twice in the first three weeks of the season and again in Week 7. Those miscues helped inspire the new system. “I had a couple early in the season, and I feel like we talked about it, but is not enough consequences that come with it other than hurting the team,” Williams said. “So [if] it hurt your pockets, maybe you’ll think about it a little more.” The penalties have become more prevalent in recent weeks, with the Patriots defense flagged for seven infractions over the last two games. On the season, New England leads the league in encroachment penalties (4), ranks fourth in neutral zone infractions (5) and is tied for the eighth-most defensive offsides penalties (3). Williams said cleaning up those small details will be an important part of the defense’s effort to bounce back after allowing a season-high 45 points to the Green Bay Packers last week. “It’s on us to be ready to go, be ready for the hard count, we’ve been jumping offsides. We’ve got to be ready for that stuff going into every game,” Williams said. “It’s costing us. We want to get teams in third and five-plus situations so we can go out there and rush. Jumping offsides is just giving them third and short, so we can’t go rush the passer.” According to Williams, any fines collected will go toward members of the team’s training staff or custodians in the building. “We’ll take care of somebody in the building. They’ll have a pretty good lunch on us, if we can’t do what we’re supposed to do,” he said. Since signing a four-year, $104 million contract with the Patriots last offseason, Williams has established himself as one of the team’s leaders. Craig Woodson was not yet aware of the fine system from his safety position, but he praised Williams for holding his teammates accountable. “I mean, that’s a leader right there,” Woodson said. “That’s something that we got to make sure that we can’t give them free yards. So, for him to do that, that’s a leader.”

New England also has a pair of candidates to return from injured reserve before Saturday’s 4 p.m. ET deadline for moves. And an open spot on the 53-man roster, too. Van Roten, a veteran of 147 NFL games along the interior line, had his 21-day practice window open last week after residing on IR due to a hamstring injury . An upgrade to full participation has followed while a fellow Patriots guard progresses through the league’s concussion protocol. And at fullback, Gilliam, who arrived on a three-year deal in March, was designated to return from a knee injury in the hours before the flight across the Atlantic Ocean. But offensive captains in tight end Hunter Henry and right tackle Morgan Moses will officially go without game designations after managing foot ailments.

title: Return to Germany an ‘unbelievable’ experience for Patriots practice squad tackle
summary: Listed at 6-foot-9, 320 pounds, Lorenz Metz is the tallest player currently under contract with the New England Patriots. Despite his towering height, however, he is largely flying under the radar. Not only is Metz is a member of the team’s practice squad, but due to his international designation ineligible to play in any games […]
full_text: Listed at 6-foot-9, 320 pounds, Lorenz Metz is the tallest player currently under contract with the New England Patriots. Despite his towering height, however, he is largely flying under the radar. Not only is Metz is a member of the team’s practice squad, but due to his international designation ineligible to play in any games this year. That will not change this week, despite the Patriots set to play the Detroit Lions just 50 miles from his hometown in the German province of Bavaria. And yet, making the trip back home and getting to practice at the facilities of FC Bayern Munich is a special experience for the 29-year-old. “I grew up about an hour from here,” he said during a press conference on Thursday. “Bayern Munich was the team. Thomas Müller, [Manuel] Neuer — all of the Bayern players were my role models. And now standing out there on the field is unbelievable.” Born in Neuötting, a city of 9,000 people east of Munich, Metz’s football journey started as a fan and somebody who couldn’t escape the Patriots even back then. “I think in 2012 they started showing regular season games in German free TV,” he explained. “2012, 2014, 2016, the Patriots were pretty much on top with Tom Brady. That was the team everybody knew, with Tom Brady, who also everybody knew.” At the age of 18, Metz started his playing career with the Kirchdorf Wildcats, appearing in 12 games and registering 48 tackles and a sack in his lone season as a defensive lineman. Shortly thereafter, he moved to the United States to play college football at Cincinnati. He switched from defensive to offensive tackle upon arrival, and over the next five seasons saw action in 39 games with 26 starts. Despite his success and being a one-time first-team All-AAC selection, Metz went unselected in the 2023 NFL Draft. He was initially picked up by the Bears as a free agent and also spent some time in Tampa before joining New England’s practice squad for the playoff run in January. Nine months later, he gets to experience the Patriots’ trip to Germany — and embracing his role as a local. Not only did he get more than 30 tickets for friends and family for Sunday’s game, he also treated his fellow offensive linemen and a handful of other teammates to dinner on Thursday night. And despite his status for the game, he is looking forward to it as well. That is especially true with his brother having visited the first ever NFL game in Munich back in 2022. “I was following it all,” he said about that particular contest between the Seahawks and Buccaneers. “I already was in college in Cinicinnati, couldn’t come to the game unfortunately, but did get two tickets for my brother. So, this is almost like a full-circle moment playing in that game and taking the field.”
