title: College Players to Watch: Week 10
summary: The Saints seem to have found a running mate for Chase Young in Carl Granderson. Right now, those two are the best pass-rushing combination in the NFL. The priority for this team should be to address the defense at every level. With that in mind, here are some important players to watch. Will Echoles remains […]
full_text: OXFORD, MS - OCTOBER 17: Ole Miss Rebels defensive tackle Will Echoles (52) celebrates a defensive stand during the game between the Ole Miss Rebels and the Missouri Tigers on October 17, 2026 at Vaught-Hemingway Stadium in Oxford, MS. (Photo by Jason Homan/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Saints seem to have found a running mate for Chase Young in Carl Granderson. Right now, those two are the best pass-rushing combination in the NFL. The priority for this team should be to address the defense at every level. With that in mind, here are some important players to watch. Will Echoles remains my favorite player for this team right now. The interior defensive lineman is arguably the best player at his position in this draft class. Right now, Echoles has 22 tackles, five TFLs, and 2.5 sacks. With the surprising lack of availability from Christen Miller, DT remains a major position of need. Echoles and the Rebels will be on the road against Oklahoma at 3:15 p.m. on the SEC Network. It goes without saying that if the run defense is not living up to expectations, then the linebackers need to be better. Well, Georgia continues to be Linebacker U, and one of the best linebackers in this class is Chris Cole. Cole is a dynamic, do-it-all linebacker for the Bulldogs. So far this season, Cole has recorded 58 tackles, 11 TFLs, five sacks, three passes defended, three fumble recoveries, and two defensive TDs. Cole is a semifinalist for both the Butkus and Lombardi Awards. Cole and the Bulldogs will be hosting Missouri at 2:30 p.m. on ABC. When talking about the run game, being able to run the ball consistently is something that can always help a marginal defense by keeping it off the field. The Saints brought back Audric Estime, and he seems to be the missing piece of the rushing offense. However, adding another running back needs to be considered, especially one who has a higher floor and ceiling than what is currently in the running back room. A player to watch should be Florida running back Jaden Baugh. Baugh currently has 860 yards on 160 carries, averaging 5.4 yards per carry while playing in the SEC on an offense that cannot throw a forward pass with confidence. He has forced 48 missed tackles and has a breakaway percentage of 44.1%. He also has 14 TDs, which leads the SEC. Baugh will be in Lexington to take on Kentucky at 5:15 p.m. on ESPN. Finally, the Saints need better play at safety. There’s no other way to describe it. A name to watch is Amare Ferrell. Ferrell is a three-year starter at safety for Indiana, and he is a consistent ball hawk. He has 11 career interceptions, including three so far this season. He’s also a solid tackler. If the Saints are getting better pressure up front, the best complement would be a safety over the top who can force incompletions or come away with interceptions. Ferrell and the Hoosiers will be hosting the USC Trojans at 2:30 p.m. on CBS. Who are some players you are excited to watch this weekend? title: Saints Rookie Report: Week 10 preview vs. the Panthers
summary: A big game is right around the corner for the New Orleans Saints, and hopefully, after the trade deadline, the rookies can lead the Saints to a win. WR Jordyn Tyson It was an exciting debut for Tyson. Yes, he fumbled on his first catch, but it was a really great play by the Browns […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - NOVEMBER 08: Jordyn Tyson #0 of the New Orleans Saints avoids a tackle Ronnie Hickman #33 of the Cleveland Browns during a game at Caesars Superdome on November 08, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images A big game is right around the corner for the New Orleans Saints, and hopefully, after the trade deadline, the rookies can lead the Saints to a win. WR Jordyn Tyson It was an exciting debut for Tyson. Yes, he fumbled on his first catch, but it was a really great play by the Browns defender, and Tyson will learn not to reach like that if he is not close enough to the end zone. But after that, when he was able to play, Tyson was open every time he was on the field and picked up some very important yards. Per head coach Kellen Moore, Tyson will have a larger role in the offense in Week 10, and he could have an incredible performance against the Panthers. DT Christen Miller I really do not know what to say anymore. Miller was a healthy scratch on Sunday. I wish there was more clarity on this situation because it makes zero sense why he is not playing. Miller has been a whelming run defender and has made little impact in pass rush, which is perfectly fine. He needs to play more. Hopefully, after the Davon Godchaux trade, Miller can have more snaps, even if he’s not the starter. TE Oscar Delp I hoped that Delp would be more involved in the offense, but that didn’t happen. Maybe if he were the receiver instead of Noah Fant on that drop, the Saints would have scored a touchdown on that play. The Saints need to start prioritizing the youth on this roster, and I’m hoping Delp can finally get some consistent targets against the Panthers. OG Jeremiah Wright News on Cesar Ruiz’s injury has not been released yet, so it’s unknown if Wright is going play, but if he does, good luck to him. The Browns defensive line is very good, and it’s going to be his biggest test yet. He wasn’t horrible against the Steelers, but it was also not good, and he looked like a rookie out there. That’s the expectation, but the Saints will need to see more from him against the Browns. WR Bryce Lance It’s time for Lance to be benched and not involved in the offense. He was thrown to once and dropped the ball, which completely stalled the drive and was outperformed by his fellow rookie WRs. Lance is a good blocker, but he’s making consistent mistakes. WR Barion Brown Now to Brown; he had a much better day. Like with Tyson, Brown made a really bad mistake that resulted in a fumble, but outside of that, he had a great day. Brown was getting the Saints in great field position on nearly every return and had a 50+ yard catch in this game. I’m hoping that Brown can take over Lance’s snaps and potentially get a few catches against the Panthers. RB CJ Donaldson Donaldson has been injured and is lower on the depth chart now. OT Mason Murphy It seems like Kelvin Banks Jr. is on his way back, so Murphy’s chances of starting become even lower. DB Lorenzo Styles Jr. As usual, Styles will likely stick with the special teams unit, but it will be interesting to see what happens if Justin Reid gets traded.

title: Our Offense vs. Their Defense: Carolina Panthers
summary: The New Orleans Saints’ offense will look to build off what was a solid outing against the Browns. The great news for the Saints is that they seem to be getting healthier at the right time. The Saints have an offense that ranks 19th in total yards, averaging 325 yards per game; 15th in scoring, […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - SEPTEMBER 27: Travis Etienne Jr. #3 of the New Orleans Saints warms up before a game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Caesars Superdome on September 27, 2026, in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints’ offense will look to build off what was a solid outing against the Browns. The great news for the Saints is that they seem to be getting healthier at the right time. The Saints have an offense that ranks 19th in total yards, averaging 325 yards per game; 15th in scoring, averaging 23.1 points per game; 26th in rushing, averaging 95.3 yards per game; and 14th in passing, averaging 230 yards per game. The Saints are actually one of the best teams on third down, converting 43.5% of their attempts, which ranks seventh in the NFL. This offense will be facing off against one of the weaker defenses in the league in the Carolina Panthers. The Panthers bring a defense that ranks below the Saints’ offense in nearly all of the aforementioned categories, except for passing yards allowed. The Panthers are allowing only 211 passing yards per game, which ranks ninth in the NFL. The area the Saints should look to attack in this game will be the running game. The Saints do not necessarily have an advantage in this area, but the Panthers are so bad at defending the run that this could be a situation where the Saints’ weakness turns into a strength. The Saints are expecting to get RB Travis Etienne Jr. back from injury, and pairing Etienne Jr. with Audric Estime may give this offense the running back duo it has been searching for since the start of the season. Carolina does not give up a lot of explosive passing plays. The Panthers are actually tied with Seattle for the fewest in the NFL, having allowed only 18. Because of how proficient their passing defense is, the Saints will need to complement the running game with a strategic passing attack that allows them to complete passes in the short and intermediate levels of the defense, forcing the Panthers’ safeties to start playing closer to the line of scrimmage. The Saints have had offensive line issues all season, and those issues could be more prevalent on Sunday, as starting center Erik McCoy will be unavailable due to a biceps injury he suffered against the Browns last week. Missing McCoy for this game could be a big loss, but getting Etienne Jr. back could almost feel like an even trade. If the Saints can run the ball with the same level of effectiveness they had against the Browns, it will help keep the Panthers’ pass rush in check. The Panthers have only 12 sacks so far this season, so neutralizing their pass rush could help make this offense more effective and potentially set the Saints up for one of their more complete performances of the season. The Panthers’ defense is not that good, but the Saints’ offense has been very inconsistent. If the Saints can score early, keep the offense balanced, and protect the football, they should leave the Dome as the No. 1 team in the NFC South on Sunday afternoon. How do you think the Saints will match up against this Panthers defense? Do you think the Saints can become the No. 1 team in the NFC South? Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: College football Week 11: Three draft prospects for the NY Giants
summary: Good morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 11 of the 2026 college football season! The college schedule is taking a bit of a breath after last week’s insane slate of games. So I want to take the time to focus on a few deep cut players who haven’t gotten much […]
full_text: Boise State running back Dylan Riley carries the ball against Colorado State. | Getty Images Good morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 11 of the 2026 college football season! The college schedule is taking a bit of a breath after last week’s insane slate of games. So I want to take the time to focus on a few deep cut players who haven’t gotten much national attention just yet, but could be real risers once the draft process gets underway. And, of course, they’ll be players at positions of (perceived) need for the Giants. We’ve spent quite a bit of time talking about defensive tackle and wide receiver, so this week I’m focusing on offensive line, defensive back, and running back. Iowa State vs. Cincinnati TNT – noon Player spotlight – Evan Tengesdahl (LG, Cincinnati) The Giants extended Jon Runyan Jr. just before the start of the 2026 season after a strong off-season and pre-season. However, he has had frustrating lapses in both pass protection and run blocking this year. The Giants might not be able to move on from Runyan easily in 2027, but it might be a good idea to have a successor in the pipeline. Tengesdahl is a big (6-foot-3, 320-pounds) mauler of a left guard who brings heavy hands and the ability to distort the line of scrimmage. He’s a solid pass protector as well as a powerful downhill run blocker, which should make him an intriguing fit in Greg Roman’s man-gap heavy run schemes. (5) Notre Dame vs. Boston College NBC – 3:30 p.m. Player spotlight – Luke Talich (S, Notre Dame) I wouldn’t ordinarily call attention to a game like this. Notre Dame should win handily against BC and this will probably be something of a snoozer. However, I wanted to take the opportunity to call attention to a player who could catch John Harbaugh’s eye in Notre Dame senior safety Luke Talich. Talich is a huge safety at 6-foot-4, 220 pounds, but also has rare versatility. His size obviously suggests a player who can thrive in the box as a pseudo-linebacker, however he has the ability to impact a game as a true “STAR” or defensive weapon. Talich currently has 43 tackles, 4.5 tackles for a loss, and a sack, which is expected for a safety of his size. What’s less expected is the fact that he leads a very good Notre Dame secondary with 3 interceptions. He also had 3 interceptions a year ago, as well as one as a sophomore. He moves surprisingly well for a player with his size and obviously has fantastic instincts for playing the ball in the air. It would be irresponsible to directly compare Talich to Kyle Hamilton, but rest assured that the “shades of…” comments will be coming once the Draft Process gets underway. And given that the Giants’ “Ravens Style” defense loves versatile defensive backs, Talich could be high on their board come draft time. (24) Boise State vs. Oregon State USA – 6pm Player Spotlight: Dylan Riley (RB, Boise State) This game has the potential to be a fun one. Boise State has been making noise lately, and they might even be a dark horse to get a College Football Playoff berth. Oregon State, meanwhile, has one of the most fun offenses in college football and freshman wideout Jesse Legree is quickly becoming a star. And since the Giants weren’t able to secure a running back to provide explosive runs at the trade deadline, I’m turning my attention to the draft. Junior running back Dylan Riley isn’t a rumbling power back at 5-foot-10, 205 pounds, but he is an absolute sparkplug with the ball in his hands. He’s currently averaging 6.7 yards per carry on 184 carries (1,241 rushing yards) with 11 rushing touchdowns — as well as 17 catches for 218 yards (12.8 per catch) and another 2 touchdowns. He has fantastic patience and vision behind the line of scrimmage, as well as a very good burst and long speed for breakaway runs. Riley also has more toughness and power than his frame would suggest, and doesn’t have a problem running between the tackles or finishing behind his pads. The Giants will be running back hunting this year, and Riley could be a much better value than a player like Jadan Baugh (Florida) or Keywan Lacey (Ole Miss) while offering similar upside.

title: Giants know why Dominic Zvada is missing kicks; now, can they fix it?
summary: New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh has steadfastly stood by rookie placekicker Dominic Zvada through Zvada’s ups and downs this season, which have included too many costly misses. Harbaugh continued to do so after Zvada’s latest miss, an extra-point distance 33-yarder in what became a three-point loss to the Washington Commanders on Thursday night. […]
full_text: Dominic Zvada after his 33-yard miss on Thursday. | Getty Images New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh has steadfastly stood by rookie placekicker Dominic Zvada through Zvada’s ups and downs this season, which have included too many costly misses. Harbaugh continued to do so after Zvada’s latest miss, an extra-point distance 33-yarder in what became a three-point loss to the Washington Commanders on Thursday night. “You can’t, as soon as a guy doesn’t make a play, start firing people left and right. Especially your kicker who’s a rookie,” Harbaugh said. “So, I’m confident he’s going to become a good kicker. I mean, at some point in time, if it doesn’t happen, it doesn’t happen. But I’m not going to panic halfway through the season when a guy’s made a bunch of kicks, if that’s what you’re inferring we should be doing. We’re just not going to knee jerk it like that. He’s going to make kicks. He’s going to make a lot of kicks. I believe in him. I think he’s really good and really talented. We’re going to give him an opportunity to do it, and it’s up to him to do it.“ Turns out, all six of Zvada’s misses this season — three pushed wide right and three yanked wide left — have come from the right hash. All 6 of Dominic Zvada’s missed kicks this season have come from the right hash, including his 33-yard miss last night. The Giants have lined up on the left hash for every extra point, where Zvada is a perfect 16/16. https://t.co/D9YzxVSYyx pic.twitter.com/UHJa8av5EK — Doug Analytics (@Doug_Analytics) November 13, 2026 “There’s a technique issue there with his plant foot that we’re kind of looking at,” Harbaugh said on Friday. “And he needs to clean that up from a consistency standpoint. He knows that. Popped up again in that one kick there. There is an issue on the right hash, no question.” Zvada was tremendous all spring and summer, beating out Ben Sauls for the placekicking job. He started the season 9-for-9, but has made just 8 of 14 kicks since. It is fair to say that Zvada’s struggles were critical parts of why the Giants tied and lost games to the Commanders, rather than winning both games. He missed three kicks in the tie to Washington in Week 5, and his miss Thursday came in a 3-point loss. It is also fair to wonder if Zvada’s struggles have impacted some of Harbaugh’s decisions. The Giants punted three times inside Washington territory Thursday night — from the 37-, 41- and 46-yard lines. Two of those kicks would have come from inside 60 yards, where the Giants have already asked Zvada to kick nine times this season. Maybe the play-calling that led to the punts would have been different if the Giants truly had faith in Zvada. Or, maybe they would have allowed him to try those kicks. “Well, let’s look at the distances. Why don’t you go back and give me the distances. I don’t have it in front of me. What were those field goals have been? They were like high 50s, weren’t they? 55 plus,” Harbaugh said. “It’s kind of a risk-reward. I’m not saying that he can’t make those kicks, but it’s a windy night and it’s a field position game in some ways. It’s a big risk there, too. Sometimes it’s better to play a field position game. “So those were toss up kind of calls probably at least, probably leaning toward punting, but I’m not saying we shouldn’t have gone for them or couldn’t have kicked them either way. The one question is, “should you have gone for it?” The next question is, “should you have kicked the field goals?” That’s the follow-up question. I don’t know. The other question could have been if we’d have missed the field goal, maybe you should have punted it down in there and played the field position game. So they’re all kind of coin flip type of decisions.” Here is how the analytics saw each of the three situations in which the Giants chose to punt rather than try the field or go for the first down: Giants 0, Commanders 0 Fourth-and-7 at the Washington 37, Q1 11:28 Commanders 17, Giants 14 Fourth-and-3 at the Washington 46, Q4 14:15 Giants 21, Commanders 17 Fourth-and-5 at the Washington 41, Q4 1:54 The point here isn’t to debate which decisions Harbaugh made correctly, and which he didn’t. Though discussing that is certainly fair game. The point is that Zvada’s continued misses are complicating the decision-making and costing the Giants points that are probably costing them games. In an NFC East race that seems likely to go down to the wire, and where every decision, every made or missed kick, everything that happens in the margins of an NFL game, could end up making the difference how much rope can the Giants give Zvada to figure it out?
author: Ed Valentine

title: New York Giants mailbag: Kickoff rule, Rasul Douglas interception, more
summary: Lou Catalano asks: Could you please explain the rule concerning kickoffs going out of bounds? In the Giants/Washington game, the ball bounced in bounds, the returner stepped out of bounds, then caught the ball while his knee was touching the ground in bounds. What ever happpened to the old John Madden maxim that one knee […]
full_text: Lou Catalano asks: Could you please explain the rule concerning kickoffs going out of bounds? In the Giants/Washington game, the ball bounced in bounds, the returner stepped out of bounds, then caught the ball while his knee was touching the ground in bounds. What ever happpened to the old John Madden maxim that one knee equals two feet? Ed says: Lou, you weren’t the only confused by this. The rulebook says: “A ball that is in player possession is out of bounds when the runner is out of bounds.” On kickoffs, this is a bit of a loophole. Credit Luke McCaffrey of the Commanders for knowing the rule and making a great play. If you plant your feet out of bounds, then touch a ball that is inbounds, it makes the ball considered to be out of bounds. That creates a kickoff out of bounds and puts the ball at the 40-yard line. I have seen this happen a couple of times. I have also seen players mess this up by either catching the ball and stepping out of bounds, or by picking the ball up inbounds right near the sideline and trying to return it. David Silver asks: I’m trying to make sense out of the last throw JJ McCarthy made to Nabers that was intercepted. It looks like McCarthy hung the ball up based on the trajectory. It also gave Nabers plenty of time to get it sighted. Douglas comes from behind to high point Nabers, but it also looked like he hit Nabers early. But that is a 50/50 ball Nabers wants. My question is, bad throw, bad catch attempt, great defensive play, or pass interference? Ed says: David, sometimes you just have to give the other guy credit. I have watched this play a bunch of times, and I listened to Nabers and John Harbaugh talk about it on Friday. Washington sent a zero blitz, rushing more players than the Giants could block and forcing J.J. McCarthy to make a split-second decision. His decision was to give the Giants’ best receiver a chance to make a play. Right decision? Wrong decision? Harbaugh just said it was the decision that McCarthy made. Douglas didn’t interfere with Nabers. Nabers said he was focused on tracking the ball and knew there was a defender in the area, but didn’t know where. Douglas did not interfere with Nabers. He just ended up making a play. The Giants have won a couple of games like that this season. The other guys get paid, too. Raymond Dansereau asks: How much better are the Giants really than last year? Last year they had a tough schedule and close losses; this year, they’re playing a weak schedule and really not always looking great. Defense seems better, but is this a 10-7 playoffs team that gets beaten badly in the first round? Or, does this look like sustainable improvement? Or too soon to say? Ed says: Raymond, I can’t go position-by-position or player-by-player in a mailbag response. I think the real answer is that the Giants are better simply because they have John Harbaugh and they are coached better. It doesn’t hurt that this team has Arvell Reese, either. The Giants are winning close games, which they couldn’t do last year. A lot of that is coaching, whether it is in-game decisions or just preparing players well enough that they believe they are supposed to make plays and win close games. If it is a 9-7-1 playoff team that gets bounced in the first round, what’s wrong with that? The Giants won seven games combined the past two seasons — a playoff berth would be a fantastic accomplishment. Sustainable improvement? The NFL is such a week-to-week and year-to-year league that is impossible to say. As long as Harbaugh is the coach, though, the Giants have a chance to be relevant. That is a massive improvement. Matt Smith asks: We’ve had four failures in a row at the head coach position. They are bookended by two Hall of Fame coaches. My question is, seeing how far the gap is between Daboll and Harbaugh, do you find it surprising how long we waited to move on from him? It seems more and more apparent to me that we had talent that we could’ve done with if we had a professional head coach with standards. The red flags were always there. Ed says: Matt, I’m not at all surprised that the Giants waited as long as they did to move on from Brian Daboll. look at the Giants’ track record: Ben McAdoo lasted less than two full seasons. Pat Shurmur was fired after two seasons. Joe Judge was fired (well, he kinda fired himself) after two seasons. You cannot get ahead when you have to keep blowing things up and starting over every two years. That means an entire new coaching staff, gutting most of the roster, and starting over. You can never institute a real philosophy or build anything that way. John Mara knew it, and he said several times that he knew he needed to be more patient than he had been. Daboll had a shockingly good first season and won Coach of the Year. The Giants could have justified firing him and GM Joe Schoen after a 3-14 2024 season, but chose not to. Mike Vrabel got hired by New England that offseason. Zero chance he was picking the Giants over the Patriots, the team he played for an an organization he loves. Ben Johnson got hired by the Bears. No chance he was picking the Giants over the Bears, who already had Caleb Williams in place. Liam Coen got hired by the Jaguars, but nobody knew that would work out as well as it had. It was really the 2025 season when it became clear that the coaching staff wasn’t maximizing the talent of the players. Adam Singer asks: During the game against the Eagles, it looked like some of the players had a diagonal line through the word “GIANTS” on their helmets while others did not. What was going on there? Ed says: Adam, the word ‘GIANTS’ was underlined. I think what you saw was the chinstrip, which buckles on the side of the helmet, protruding over the lettering on some of the helmets. Ronald Lukoff asks: I usually do not disagree with a lot of your comments but I do take exception to your thoughts about the Giants making a blockbuster trade today (this is written Tuesday morning). I have been a Giant fan since 1956. I have seen a lot of success and a lot of failure. This team is made up of a lot of draft picks and I really do not want to give up future draft choices for a player that can give us a division title. This team has only played one team with a record above .500. Do you really think that one player is worth losing draft capital? If I thought one player could get us to the Super Bowl, I might feel differently. Do you think JJ is the answer at QB. He was great first 5 quarters, not so much last game. but a quarterback needy ream just traded him away, so I am hesitant to put all my faith in him and believe me, I hope I’m wrong. I feel like we are at least a year away from potentially going to the Super Bowl and while I would love to win the division, I just don’t think giving up draft choices is the best way to build a championship team. You’re feelings? Ed says: Ronald, it’s moot at this point since the trade deadline has come and gone. I want to clarify this, anyway. I wrote earlier in the week that the Giants should try to capitalize on the opportunity they have in the NFC East. You don’t know if or when that opportunity will come again. They did try to do that. They were very aggressive. They were also careful. I said earlier in the week there was a price they should not go to — meaning they should not go above the second-round pick they had offered the Colts for Jonathan Taylor. They — rightly — refused to do that. I said all along the end game is not winning the division this year and then going back to being a third- or fourth-place team for fove years after that. The end game is to be a championship contender on a consistent basis. You have to protect your future to do that.
author: Ed Valentine

title: NY Giants news: Reactions to Washington loss, J.J. McCarthy, more
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know this weekend. Giants embrace upcoming gauntlet: ‘We want all the smoke’ | NJ.com The Giants will be rooting hard for the 49ers this weekend. That’s because if the Cowboys somehow beat San Francisco, they’ll move closer to the Giants in the […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know this weekend. Giants embrace upcoming gauntlet: ‘We want all the smoke’ | NJ.com The Giants will be rooting hard for the 49ers this weekend. That’s because if the Cowboys somehow beat San Francisco, they’ll move closer to the Giants in the NFC East race. The Giants are 5-3-1 after Thursday night’s 24-21 gut-punch loss to the Commanders. Coach John Harbaugh’s team remains alone atop the division, ahead of the 4-5 Cowboys and 3-5-1 Commanders (who now have the head-to-head tiebreaker edge over the Giants). On to the next one J.J. McCarthy on moving forward after Thursday night pic.twitter.com/7Z2MNx8u4e — New York Giants (@Giants) November 13, 2026 Why J.J. McCarthy kept chucking ball downfield before game-sealing interception in Giants’ crushing loss | New York Post Quarterback J.J. McCarthy certainly shouldn’t shoulder all the blame, but an interception with 25 seconds remaining in the fourth quarter sealed the loss and gave the Commanders the tiebreaker over the Giants after the two teams tied in Week 5. Despite being at the Washington 48-yard line with 40 seconds remaining and needing only a field goal, McCarthy threw deep on his final two passes. The first fell to the turf for an incomplete pass, and the second was intended for Malik Nabers but instead landed in Rasul Douglas’ arms to end the Giants’ comeback attempt. “My thought process was pop it up to my playmakers, have them go make a play,” McCarthy said. What we saw as NY Giants fail to seal the deal against Commanders | The Record For the first time all season, the New York Giants failed to deliver with the lead in the fourth quarter and the game on the line. Jayden Daniels’ third touchdown pass, this one to Stefon Diggs, as two Giants defenders ran into each other with 57 seconds remaining allowed Washington to snap Big Blue’s two-game winning streak with a 24-21 victory at MetLife Stadium. Cam Skattebo scores twice after Giants’ quiet trade deadline, but wonders if he could’ve done more in loss to Commanders | New York Daily News But after the Giants’ offense stagnated down the stretch of a 24-21 loss — with Jameis Winston and J.J. McCarthy both getting stopped on third-down QB keepers — Skattebo was left wondering if he could have done more. “It sucks, and I think part of it is I put myself in a situation last time we played these guys that kind of killed the trust in Coach [John Harbaugh] maybe a little bit, of giving up the ball last time,” Skattebo said. “And maybe he didn’t want to give me the ball again. I don’t know. I’m not gonna say that was something that he was thinking, but I would think that as well.” Skattebo followed with runs of five and two yards, setting up a crucial 3rd and 3. But on a designed QB run, McCarthy was tackled by Sonny Styles behind the line of scrimmage, prompting another Giants punt. Asked if he felt he could have led the Giants into field-goal range had he gotten the ball, Skattebo replied, “I can’t say that. Do I think that? Yeah, but I can’t say that, because it could’ve been any situation at any time.” New York Giants slam ‘corny’ DPI penalty called on Deonte Banks | USAToday.com “This league is funny, bro,” said Safety Tyler Nubin. “This league is funny. There’s really nothing you can do about it, man. When you’re in trail position, nine times out of 10, they’re going to call that PI. That’s just how the league is. Just got to weather it.” “I’m going to be honest, and I ain’t going to say nothing that gets me fined,” Safety Jason Pinnock said. “But it’s getting to a point now where [offensive coordinators] are taking advantage of it. They’re not calling real plays. They’re going four wide, and they’re throwing that junk outside. And it looks like these receivers literally have techniques to get PIs. They’re grabbing the back of DBs’ necks. It’s almost like it’s becoming a technique.” The window that J.J. McCarthy put this in…. On 3rd & 7.. this should've been the defining pass play in a win pic.twitter.com/4xqG4zB3jr — Dan Schneier (@DanSchneierNFL) November 13, 2026 2026 NFL midseason award rankings: MVP picks, top rookies, OPOY, DPOY, coaches | ESPN.com Defensive Rookie of the Year. 1. Arvell Reese, LB/Edge, New York Giants. Picking between Bailey and Reese is unfair. I leaned Reese if only because he has been two impactful players in one this season. As an off-ball linebacker, Reese has been all over the place for a Giants team that has been better against the run this season, even after trading Dexter Lawrence II. Reese has made tackles on 15.3% of his snaps, the eighth-highest rate in the league. He has given up an 81.3 passer rating in coverage, a very credible number for a veteran linebacker, let alone a rookie just getting his feet wet at this level. And then there’s Reese’s side quest as a devastating force on blitzes. Despite rushing the quarterback only about 11 times per game, Reese already has 4.5 sacks and 14 pressures. His 10.2% quick pressure rate would be the second-best mark in the NFL if he qualified. And the average Reese pressure comes after 2.44 seconds, the fifth fastest among players with 10 pressures or more. NFL midseason superlatives and lessons: Josh Allen for MVP, all-in moves, dashed hopes | The Athletic Defensive rookie of the year – LB Arvell Reese, New York Giants. The No. 5 pick in the 2026 NFL Draft has racked up 4.5 sacks, eight tackles for loss, 49 solo tackles (68 total), a forced fumble and an interception for the surprising Giants. Coach of the Year — John Harbaugh, New York Giants. Ben Johnson continues to lead an impressive Chicago Bears team, and Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers rank among the Super Bowl favorites. But with the Giants unexpectedly leading their division and contending for their first playoff berth since the 2022 season — with a backup quarterback, no less — Harbaugh gets the nod. 2026 NFL DROY Odds: Which New York Rookie Has The Edge? | FOX Sports Arvell Reese has jumped David Bailey on the odds board and sits at +100 after Week 9. The Giants rookie was drafted with the fifth pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, and so far, he’s exceeding those expectations. Through nine weeks, Reese is second in the entire NFL in solo tackles (49) and leads the Giants’ defense in total tackles as a rookie. Reese joined Nick Bosa (2019) as the only players in the last 25 seasons with at least four sacks, an interception, a forced fumble and a fumble recovery in their first eight career games. It looks like the G-Men have finally found a guy they can build their defense around for the next decade. NFL midseason awards: The good, the bad and the Dallas Cowboys | Yahoo! Sports The ‘Chicken Salad from Chicken S**t’ Award: New York Giants. Boy, the Giants were feeling fine after their Week 1 win over Dallas. And just as quickly, hopes deflated when Jaxson Dart went down with a season-ending injury in Week 2. But somehow, the Giants have cobbled together win after win, using quarterback after quarterback, and suddenly they’re dangerous. Granted, it’s a “is that stray dog going to beg for food or bite my face?” kind of dangerous, but it’s better than nothing. title: Malik Nabers ‘not really aware’ of where Washington DB was on decisive interception
summary: New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers on Friday responded to criticism of the idea that he could have given a better effort to knock the ball down on a game-ending interception by Rasul Douglas of the Washington Commanders on Thursday night in the Giants’ 24-21 loss. “Seeing the ball go up at the time, […]
full_text: New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers on Friday responded to criticism of the idea that he could have given a better effort to knock the ball down on a game-ending interception by Rasul Douglas of the Washington Commanders on Thursday night in the Giants’ 24-21 loss. “Seeing the ball go up at the time, didn’t really see him [Douglas] or where he was, so I’m not really aware of that,” Nabers said. “My head is looking up at the ball, even though he was driving on the ball. So, just seeing how high the ball was and just waiting for it to come down and made a jump to catch the ball and then got hit and then he made a play.” Here is the play: RASUL DOUGLAS CALLS GAME. pic.twitter.com/5q7ahQYaoa — NFL (@NFL) November 13, 2026 Nabers was not available to media in the post-game locker room. He said he had a “family emergency back home” that he had to deal with, but that “it’s straight” now. The Giants, at Washington’s 48-yard line in the closing minute, took back-to-back deep shots. Head coach John Harbaugh said “zero blitzes” by the Commanders led to quarterback J.J. McCarthy taking those shots. Nabers indicated the deep throw might not have been the ideal result. “I think as far as that play and in the ending of the game, I’d say we will be better on just finding a better situation on not trying to score points as quickly as we were, but just make smart decisions on what we want to get to after seeing the cover zero that it was giving us at the moment,” Nabers said. “So, trying to just get the ball out fast instead of trying to create a home run ball. So, you just got to be better in the situation, and that’s really all.” Nabers fumbled at the Washington 15-yard line with the Giants trailing 17-14 in the third quarter. That was one of many scoring opportunities the Giants did not capitalize on Thursday night. “You’re thinking about plays that could have been a difference in the game, and that could have been one of those,” Nabers said. “We were in the red zone, could have got a field goal or a touchdown, and sadly went away just off a mistake that I made. But I mean, just try to do better, try to be better, and I’ll be better on just protecting the football, having awareness of where I am, and just like I said, protecting the football to give the offense opportunity to score points on that drive.” Nabers and Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels were LSU teammates and remain close friends. Nabers aid it was “bugging me pretty bad” that he has never beaten Daniels as a pro. “He calls me all the time,” Nabers said. “He’s probably trying to call me right now, but I can’t answer that phone call.” Nabers said he has a hard time letting go of lost games. “Every loss stings. Every loss I think we go through, it stings and it hurts, but you got to have your own flush mindset,” he said. “It’s just, we lost, okay, let’s focus on how to win the next one. Let’s focus on doing the things better that we made mistakes on and we bummed out about the loss, but we continue to try to put it behind us and keep going forward and try to get a win next week. “I’m still trying to find ways, like I said, I take losses more painful than I say a lot of people just because overall I want to win so bad. So, when I receive a loss, I just, I don’t know, it hurts. But it’s the NFL, 16 teams a week are going to lose the game. So, you just got to come to the realization that it’s going to happen. You just got to be able to flush it and just move on and just fight back and try to go get a win, try to do everything that you can the next week to try to get a win. So, it’s hard for sure but I don’t know how to handle that. I’m still going through that. I’m still learning, try to find my way on flushing losses like this or just flushing a loss in general. So, I don’t I don’t know how to answer that question because I’m still learning from it, still learning how to do that.”
author: Ed Valentine

title: PFF grades and advanced stats from the Giants’ loss to the Commanders
summary: The post-mortem on a game the New York Giants should have won but didn’t is never fun. Let’s see what we can learn from the Pro Football Focus grades and advanced stats about who played well and who didn’t. Before looking at the offense and defense, let’s note that PFF gave Jordan Stout his lowest […]
full_text: Ar’Darius Washington celebrates a defensive stop with Greg Newsome | Getty Images The post-mortem on a game the New York Giants should have won but didn’t is never fun. Let’s see what we can learn from the Pro Football Focus grades and advanced stats about who played well and who didn’t. Before looking at the offense and defense, let’s note that PFF gave Jordan Stout his lowest grade of the season because of that 12-yard shank in the fourth quarter that gave the Commanders decent field position to start their winning drive, and of course Dominic Zvada got a low grade for his field goal miss from 32 yards out (though not as low as the first Washington and the Houston games in which he had multiple misses). That’s part of the story, but there was blame to go around on the offense and defense. And let’s not forget the coaching. In the old days we used to speak of a “prevent defense” that tried to hold a lead by playing soft coverage that stopped big plays. Well, last night John Harbaugh played what might be called a “prevent offense,” being scared off field goal attempts and punting in Commanders’ territory after Zvada’a early miss and trying to wind down the clock with running plays and quarterback keepers instead of calling easy pitch-and-catch plays to keep the ball out of Jayden Daniels’ hands. PFF grades: Offense PFF did not give a single elite (80 or higher) grade to anyone on the offense last night (part of that was due to the weather conditions, Washington only had one elite-graded offensive player themselves, Ben Sinnott). J.J. McCarthy received an overall very good offense grade, more because of his running (three scrambles for 29 yards) than his passing. However, his passing grade was brought down by his final offensive play, an interception deep downfield on which he was blitzed and on which Malik Nabers did not make much of an effort to help him out. Overall, J.J. handled the pressure well, doing about as well as when he was kept clean: J.J. was blitzed on 45% of dropbacks: 2 of his 3 turnover-worthy plays came on blitzes, but 2 of his 3 big-time throws also came on blitzes. Overall, with 293 yards, a pretty good performance. Of note is the performance of the offensive line. Even though McCarthy was pressured on 35% of his dropbacks, the OL performed pretty well overall. Jon Runyan and Sisi Mauigoa had great pass-blocking games, Runyan having a clean stat line and Mauigoa only giving up one hurry. The run block grades weren’t as good but not terrible either. Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor both graded very good in pass coverage with 2 hurries charged to AT and one QB hit to Eluemunor. Bryan Hudson graded below average in pass blocking with 2 hurries and just barely below average in run blocking. Patrick Ricard had his best game as a Giant, especially in run blocking. Cam Skattebo fell just below the Very Good category with his 18 rushes for 78 yards; maybe he was graded down a bit for eating before the game and throwing up on the sideline 🙂 None of the receivers graded as high as Very Good, though Malachi Fields and Isaiah Likely came close. The reason Likely didn’t grade higher despite his 9 of 11, 127 yard, 1 TD performance was because of his fumble; PFF grades turnovers very severely. Malik Nabers only had 44 yards on 5 catches in 7 targets, but his very low grade reflects his fumble which cost the Giants a scoring opportunity. PFF grades: Defense The defense was a different story. There was one excellent defensive performance last night – the defense was not the main reason the Giants lost the game. Ar’Darius Washington has seen his playing time increase the past three weeks, and last night he graded an outstanding 89.9 overall, 91.4 in coverage. Washington was targeted 6 times and gave up 3 completions for a total of only 11 yards and a 16.7 passer rating. He made back-to-back great plays, a pass reception stop and then an interception, with the game on the line and the Commanders in scoring position. His only blemish was 3 missed tackles, but he did have 5 tackles and 2 assists. The rest of the secondary did not perform as well. Deonte Banks received a barely below average coverage and overall defense grade; if he turns his head and tries to play the ball on the deep pass to Treylon Burks with less than two minutes left in the game, there’s no flag and the Giants may end up winning the game. Jevon Holland had the big interception, but he also gave up a TD and 40 yards total on pass plays. Dru Phillips graded 53.5 overall and 48.8 in coverage primarily because he gave up the game-losing TD to Stefon Diggs, but he also missed two tackles. Greg Newsome also graded below average, giving up 22 yards on 2 receptions in 3 targets and missing a tackle. Jason Pinnock graded low as well before leaving the game; he missed 2 tackles and graded low in coverage, primarily because he was covering on the Daniels TD pass to Ben Sinnott. The Giants’ most high profile defensive players (with Brian Burns out for the season) are now Abdul Carter and Arvell Reese. Both were graded Very Good overall by PFF. Reese did nothing in the pass rush last night, but he did have 7 tackles and 5 assists, three of them stops, with no missed tackles. He also gave up four completions in four targets in pass coverage, but they only went for 21 yards total with only 9 YAC, warranting a Very Good coverage grade. Carter is the more difficult evaluation. He continues to be unable to get to the QB for sacks, but he did have a QB hit and 2 hurries plus 2 tackles and an assist, resulting in a Very Good overall defense grade. Micah McFadden had a QB hurry and 9 tackles plus an assist, but he only graded average overall because he surrendered 4 catches and 55 yards on pass defense. The rest of the defensive line was a bunch of mediocre to poor performances. Kayvon Thibodeaux only had one QB hurry and graded fairly low on run defense despite 7 tackles and an assist, suggesting that he was just blocked out of some running plays. D.J. Reader had his worst game as a Giant, with only 1 hurry and 1 tackle. Shelby Harris got his first sack and had a hurry and 2 tackles, 2 assists. Bobby Jamison-Travis continues to get snaps but had only a tackle and an assist, but that was better than Darius Alexander, who only had one tackle. Advanced stats The Giants’ defense overall can be summed up as: Not bad, but not great either. Here is an overall ranking of NFL defenses in a number of categories: Defensive Stats through Week 9 (ranked by PPG allowed) pic.twitter.com/nOqfj6MuHF — SFdata9ers🏈📊 (@sfdata9ers) November 13, 2026 Overall, the Giants rank No. 12 in the NFL in points per game given up. That sounds pretty good, although you would have to say that other than the Rams, they haven’t played any of the NFL’s powerhouse offenses. They are below average in sacks, slightly below average in takeaways, and among the league’s worst in tackles for loss. It could be a lot worse, but they don’t scare anyone either. Speaking of scaring, note that the Jaguars, next week’s opponent, are No. 2 in the league in points per game allowed despite not scoring high in any individual category, unlike the No. 1 Vikings, who rank highest in sacks. Somehow the Jags are keeping teams out of the end zone in most of their games. They have the second best red zone D in the NFL, while the Giants’ red zone D is near the bottom: Red Zone Defense Rankings pic.twitter.com/PKXKlBoGMH — SFdata9ers🏈📊 (@sfdata9ers) November 13, 2026 That matters, because as I have noted, John Harbaugh and his offensive coordinator Matt Nagy have mostly been very conservative in their play calling and fourth down decisions. That’s quantified below by Kevin Cole of Unexpected Points: Latest @Unexpected_Pts Data Debunk: John Harbaugh lost his fourth-down mojo and it’s costing the Giants Harbaugh was one most aggressive fourth-down decision-makers with the Ravens, not so much this season with the Giants Link in reply…

title: Giants-Commanders: 5 plays that led to the loss
summary: The New York Giants lost a close home game to the Washington Commanders, 24-21. New York’s defense forced two interceptions in the fourth quarter — with a four-point lead— but the Giants’ offense went three-and-out on both drives, resulting in an opportunistic Washington score that secured the win for the Commanders. John Harbaugh used the […]
full_text: Rasul Douglas seals the game for Washington with an interception. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants lost a close home game to the Washington Commanders, 24-21. New York’s defense forced two interceptions in the fourth quarter — with a four-point lead— but the Giants’ offense went three-and-out on both drives, resulting in an opportunistic Washington score that secured the win for the Commanders. John Harbaugh used the apt word “disappointing” to describe the loss. New York was on the precipice of a commanding lead in the NFC East, but Washington now owns the tiebreaker between the two teams, even though New York leads the standings by two games. Losing home games in the division is tough, and something that’s very familiar to Giants fans, unfortunately. Still, the Giants do lead the division and have a tough stretch of opponents remaining on their schedule. They have two home games against the Jaguars and the 49ers in the next three weeks ( a game against the Colts in between ), as well as a trip out to Seattle. This season is FAR from over, but a win against Washington would have been a welcome, comfortable result. Here are five plays that led to the loss. Play(s) 1: Three-play sequence This was a three-play sequence in the fourth quarter where EACH side of the football failed miserably. Firstly, the defense shouldn’t bear much blame for this loss; they forced two interceptions and a turnover on downs in the fourth quarter. It’s the offense that couldn’t pick up a yard and was stopped multiple times on third down when it mattered most, but I digress back to my point… The third-and-3 quarterback sweep where Sonny Styles tackled J.J. McCarthy for a loss of two was the first of this terrible sequence: Sonny Styles said absolutely not on 3rd down. WASvsNYG on Prime Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/1d9S7zwsT3 — NFL (@NFL) November 13, 2026 Ar’Darius Washington intercepted Daniels with 2:19 left on the clock; 29 seconds later, the Giants are punting after three offensive plays for the second consecutive drive after an interception. I don’t like the call at all, but the failed third-down conversion attempt was made much worse by a rare terrible moment from punter Jordan Stout. Stout punted the football 12 YARDs from Washington’s 41-yard line to their 29 — an inexcusable mistake. New York couldn’t consider a 58-yard field goal attempt from Dominic Zvada, who missed a 33-yarder on New York’s second drive, so special teams’ unreliability compounded the problem, and this punt gave Washington solid field position. The third play, though, WAS on the defense. Tae Banks committed a defensive pass interference against Treylon Burks, which gave Washington the ball at the New York 38-yard line with a minute and a half to go in the 21-17 Giants’ game. Two plays later, the game was 24-21, Washington. Play 2: Stefon Diggs STEFON DIGGS TOUCHDOWN "IM LIKE DAT" pic.twitter.com/IIFy2fEOLL — wok (@wokdior) November 13, 2026 The Giants forced a third-and-4 with just over a minute left in the game, and New York rushed seven, initially, dropping two defensive linemen off a half-second after the snap. Jaydon Daniels threw it right past the Giants’ defensive lineman to Stefon Diggs (3), who had inside leverage against Dru Phillips (22). Phillips fell and took out Tae Banks (2), allowing Diggs to walk into the end zone. The Giants capitulated the lead after several fourth-quarter plays that gave them opportunities to seal the victory. New York received the football back, though… Play 3: Game-sealing interception Rasul Douglas Picks Off JJ McCarthy's Last Throw Of The Game And Waves Goodbye To The Giants Fans. We've Seen Him Make A Game-Winning Interception And Wave Goodbye To Fans On A Thursday Night Before. Don't Let Green Bay Packers Fans See This. pic.twitter.com/fQZGlt470W — SM Highlights (@SMHighlights1) November 13, 2026 Washington ran Cover-0 on this third-and-10 with 33 seconds left in the game. J.J. McCarthy (18) had to heave the ball under pressure, taking a big hit in the process. New York was attempting to hit Malik Nabers (1) on the slot fade against Amik Robertson (2). Isaiah Likely (9) ran a quick curl and Malachi Fields (88) stayed on the line of scrimmage, which — in theory — would have given the Giants a true one-on-one matchup with Nabers against Robertson, but Rasual Douglas (29) had something else planned. Douglas played off Fields with an inside turn, looking through the No.2 and No. 3 receivers ( inner receivers, Nabers and Likely ). Robertson read McCarthy and carried Nabers vertical, giving Robertson support on the outside. The ball was underthrown and thrown with a high trajectory, which allowed Douglas to squeeze Nabers’ slot vertical; in doing so, he undercut the route and intercepted the pass. Washington made a wise play by having Douglas play at depth and leverage to read Nabers’ route and help his teammate on the vertical, despite being assigned to Fields. It’s also something the Giants can learn from. Washington knew this from tape study, since New York runs the same slot-fade with the outside receiver staying put on the line of scrimmage. Play 4: Dominic Zvada continues to struggle The Giants had two solid offensive drives to start the game. On their first drive, New York punted from the Washington 42-yard line after taking a delay of game on a fourth-and-7 from the 37-yard line. They played the game of field position and did not attempt a 54-yard field goal. The Giants then got Zvada into a position to hit a 33-yard field goal, and the rookie kicker missed it wide left. It’s just inexcusable. "The rookie out of Michigan had his issues but Harbaugh stayed with him" Dominic Zvada proceeds to miss the 33-yarder. Harbaugh did not look happy. We are still all tied up in New York! pic.twitter.com/U2N0LSjCUq — Chat Sports (@ChatSports) November 13, 2026 TWO solid Giants’ drives yield ZERO points because of the kicker, with one ending in the 33-yard miss above. John Harbaugh provided confidence to the media when discussing Zvada after the game, but these missed kicks by Giants’ kickers are an all-too-familiar occurrence that is now persisting with the undrafted rookie kicker out of Michigan. Play(s) 5: End of first half The Giants ended their first half by surrendering a nine-play, 67-yard drive that ended in this 1-yard touchdown catch by Ben Sinnott: BEN SINNOTT…TOLD YOU https://t.co/EP7lZbvOU5 pic.twitter.com/fh1yOGHV9r — Tanner Phifer (@TannerPhifer) November 13, 2026 All three of Washington’s touchdowns were on third down for Washington: the Ben Sinnott and Stefon Diggs’ ones above, and the 31-yarder to Antonio Williams. The one to Sinnott, though, was in the final seconds of the first half. The Giants’ defense surrendered the drive, and Washington bled the clock perfectly to not provide the Giants an opportunity to drive down the field for points. It was excellently handled by Washington. BONUS An unfortunate bonus play makes the cut here. New York scored a touchdown on their first drive of the second half after the Giants’ defense responded to the end of the first half with a three-and-out that lost 15 yards—wow! Unfortunately, Washington had an answer with a third-and-1 31-yard strike to Antonio Williams. that gave Washington a 17-14 lead. New York, though, drove the football down the field on a five-play, 53-yard drive, with a big 16-yard catch to Malachi Fields on a second-and-seven. McCarthy then completed a pass to Nabers for three-yards on a second-and-12 at the Washington 19-yard line, and Nabers allowed the ball to get punched out of his grasp. It was a red zone trip that ended in a turnover. Luckily the Giants’ defense forced a three-and-out, but New York’s offense punted the football — yet again — from Washington’s territory.

title: Giants try to keep perspective, but this was a massive missed opportunity
summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — You wanted them to, of course. Did you really think, though, that the New York Giants were just going to waltz to the NFC East title without things getting interesting? The Giants made things interesting, and much more convoluted, by losing to the Washington Commanders on Thursday and missing an opportunity […]
full_text: The Giants celebrated this Jevon Holland interception, but the Commanders got the final celebration on Thursday night. | Getty Images EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — You wanted them to, of course. Did you really think, though, that the New York Giants were just going to waltz to the NFC East title without things getting interesting? The Giants made things interesting, and much more convoluted, by losing to the Washington Commanders on Thursday and missing an opportunity to take firm control of the division. The 5-3-1 Giants are still in first place, and will remain there through the weekend no matter how the second-place Dallas Cowboys fare on Sunday when they host the 7-1 San Francisco 49ers. Their path to a first division title since the 2011 Super Bowl season is now much more difficult, and uncertain. If the Cowboys can upset the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday, they will be 5-5, just 1.5 games behind the Giants with eight weeks left in the season. The Commanders are now 3-5-1, and with a tiebreaker advantage over the Giants should also feel like their season is very much alive. ‘You’re going to lose some games’ Giants head coach John Harbaugh called the loss “disappointing”, a word he used multiple times in his post-game press conference. His tone, though, was meant to remind that the Giants had not suddenly turned into the Titanic. “It’s a missed opportunity, but like I told the guys, it would have been great to win the game, but it doesn’t change our goals or our opportunity going forward,” head coach John Harbaugh said after the game. “So, it’s a tough loss. It’s the National Football League. You’re going to lose some games. And everybody in this league is good. The Commanders are good. Everybody’s good. So, I mean, we have a really good team coming in here next Sunday [the Jacksonville Jaguars]. A team that we can beat, so, we’ve just got to get back to work. “It’s disappointing, yeah. I mean, I think that’s the best word. It’s just disappointing, We worked hard for this, and we put a hard week in. And we were prepared. The guys came out with, I thought, tremendous energy. We played very hard. Plays were made. Plays were missed. But it wasn’t good enough to win the game. And that’s the disappointment of it. So it’s disappointing, but you can’t let it bring you down. That’s why I said what I said about our spirit. Our spirit’s going to be fine. We’re going to be good. We’re not going to curl up. We’re going to come out fighting.” In his 19th season as a head coach, it was clear that Harbaugh wanted to project an image of calm amidst the storm. “It would have been nice to open up a lead in the division. We didn’t open it up as much as we could have if we had got the win. We’ve got a lot of tough games. What do we have, seven games left? [It’s actually eight] So it’s going to be seven dogfights. That’s what it’s going to be,” Harbaugh said. “It’s [the] National Football League. I’d like to say we’re going to win all seven of them. But it’s probably not very likely. You’re probably not going to be putting any money down on that. “So we’ve got to win enough. And this was one that got away. We’ve got to find a way to get the next one. And the next one after that. And the next one after that. And get as many as we need to win the division. That’s what we’ve got to find a way to do. So just try to keep it in perspective is very important.” Players echoed the coach. “This game would have obviously put us in a great lead in the division, but we’re not dead,” fullback Patrick Ricard said. “This division can still be won.” “This would have obviously helped us to get the division sooner, but that’s still well in our grasp,” said center Bryan Hudson. Death by a thousand paper cuts That is kind of what this game felt like. From the beginning things did not go according to plan. The Giants, somehow, managed to possess the ball in Washington territory six times without coming up with a point. Let’s go through the litany of miscues and missed chances. They surprisingly chose to take the ball after winning the pre-game coin toss. They drove to the Commanders’ 37-yard line, but an Isaiah Likely drop ended the drive. Rather than go for it or try a 55-yard field goal, the Giants punted. The Giants second drive stalled at the Washington 15-yard line, and Dominic Zvada [more on him later] missed a 33-yard field goal. In the third quarter, the Giants reached the Washington 19-yard line only to have Malik Nabers fumble the ball away after catching a short pass. On their first possession of the fourth quarter, the Giants punted on fourth-and-3 from the Washington 46-yard line. That came after a third-down drop by Theo Johnson, and analytics disagreed with Harbaugh’s decision: Honestly, so did I. I would rather have seen the Giants go for it there, especially trailing. My preference? Run the ball on third down and then go for it on fourth if you don’t make the first down. It seemed clear from the play call, though, that Harbaugh did not see that spot as two-down, fo-for-it territory. The Giants had two chances to ice the game in the final 5:27 after interceptions by safeties Jevon Holland at the Giants’ 2-yard line and Ar’Darius Washington at the Commanders’ 46-yard line. They could not generate a single first down on either occasion. Washington coach Dan Quinn successfully challenged a Jameis Winston tush push that was initially ruled a first down on the first possession, forcing a Giants punt. The Giants caught a bad break to open that drive when Holland was ruled down at the 2-yard line after his interception, rather than in the end zone. A touchback would have given the Giants the ball at the 20-yard line. On the second one, J.J. McCarthy was dropped for a loss on a designed quarterback run on third-and-3 from the Commanders’ 39-yard line. Instead of pretty much being able to run out the clock, the Giants punted. Jordan Stout exacerbated the failure with a terrible 12-yard punt, his first bad punt as a Giant. On their final desperation drive, the Giants got to Washington’s 48-yard line before a McCarthy deep pass intended for Nabers was intercepted. The defense was hardly beyond reproach. After the Giants took a 10-7 lead with 2:35 left in the half, the Giants allowed Washington to run out the rest of the half with a nine-play, 67-yard drive that ended with a 1-yard touchdown pass to Ben Sinnott, giving the Commanders a 14-7 halftime lead. The Giants’ pass rush was virtually non-existent. They got one sacks and two hits on Jayden Daniels. On their final drive, Washington went 71 yards for the game-winning score in just three plays and :49 seconds. Oh, those missed field goals Zvada is now just 17 of 23 (73.9%) after Thursday night’s miss, which was from extra-point distance. Misses by Zvada in both Washington games (three in Week 5) have proven costly. Dominic Zvada misses a 33-yarder and John Harbaugh looks on in disappointment pic.twitter.com/nC0zKf3trH — Talkin’ Giants (@TalkinGiants) November 13, 2026 After the game, Harbaugh tried to remain supportive of his rookie kicker. “We’re confident. You can’t, as soon as a guy doesn’t make a play, start firing people left and right. Especially your kicker who’s a rookie,” Harbaugh said. “So, I’m confident he’s going to become a good kicker. I mean, at some point in time, if it doesn’t happen, it doesn’t happen. But I’m not going to panic halfway through the season when a guy’s made a bunch of kicks, if that’s what you’re inferring we should be doing. “So, I mean, we’re just not going to knee jerk it like that. He’s going to make kicks. He’s going to make a lot of kicks. I believe in him. I think he’s really good and really talented. We’re going to give him an opportunity to do it, and it’s up to him to do it. At some point, though, it’s not a knee-jerk reaction. Harbaugh lost his job in Baltimore last season in part because rookie placekicker Tyler Loop missed a field goal that would have put the Ravens into the playoffs. As…

title: A scoop and score is long overdue for the Jets
summary: The Jets’ defense has had its issues in 2026, to say the least. However, there’s at least one area where they have improved. The defense as a whole has been a lot more opportunistic this year in terms of forcing fumbles. Led by David Bailey’s five, they have forced a total of 13 fumbles. That’s […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - OCTOBER 18: David Bailey #31 of the New York Jets tackles Treveyon Henderson #32 of the New England Patriots during the third quarter at Gillette Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Maddie Meyer/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jets’ defense has had its issues in 2026, to say the least. However, there’s at least one area where they have improved. The defense as a whole has been a lot more opportunistic this year in terms of forcing fumbles. Led by David Bailey’s five, they have forced a total of 13 fumbles. That’s already four more than the total for all of last season. New York’s fumble luck has been a lot better too, as they’ve recovered 50 percent of all fumbles. This is much higher than their 2025 percentage, which was the second-worst in the league at 35 percent (and was actually on target to break the all-time record until they had a few over the last few weeks of the season). Had they been closer to 50 percent last year, or 2023 when they were dead last in fumble recovery percentage, or 2022 when they were 30th, those seasons could arguably have played out very differently. 2023 in particular was particularly galling, as the Jets started 7-4 and then lost their last six as the turnovers dried up. They almost tied the all-time NFL record for the fewest defensive fumble recoveries until Carl Lawson ended a nine-game drought by recovering one with two games remaining. In the end, they only managed to recover 21 percent of fumbles by opposing offenses. It’s often been debated how much of fumble recovery percentages are dictated by talent and how much is based on luck, with most analytical studies concluding it’s mostly luck. However, if you have a team that is hungry and hustles to the ball, has players who are particularly adept at possessing loose balls or are creating the kinds of fumbles which are more likely to be recovered by the defense, this obviously has an effect on some level. Regardless, at least the Jets have seemingly started to regress to the mean in this area. So the next question becomes when will they start to do anything impactful with these recoveries? This Thursday marked the 14th anniversary of the last time a Jets defensive player recovered a ball off the turf and returned it for a touchdown. That was Muhammad Wilkerson, on a play where Mike DeVito had forced the ball loose on a sack of Russell Wilson. That’s a pretty remarkable statistic. Although there have only been six fumble returns for touchdowns in the first nine weeks of this NFL season, the Jets averaged over eight fumble returns per decade in the 80’s, 90’s and 2000’s. Doesn’t it feel like they’re long overdue? Wilkerson’s touchdown was not actually the last defensive fumble return for a touchdown by the Jets. Jamal Adams officially owns that distinction, on a memorable play where he ripped the ball out of Daniel Jones’ hands and ran it in. He therefore didn’t recover it off the ground, so it wasn’t a conventional scoop and score. Even this was a far-too-long seven years ago. Since 2012, the Jets have also scored three other touchdowns on fumbles but two (Matt Slauson and Charone Peake) were on offense, and the other was a muffed punt recovered in the end zone by Art Maulet. Again, none of these was in the past seven years. The Jets’ last defensive touchdown was a pick-six by Jermaine Johnson and that one dates back to 2023. It feels like a scoop and score is exactly the kind of momentum-shifting play that has been lacking ever since Aaron Glenn took over as head coach. It’s the kind of thing that could give them a chance to upset a favored opponent, which is something Glenn’s team probably needs to do a couple of times between now and the end of the season if he wants to mount a strong enough case to return for a third year. With Bailey in particular doing a good job of creating these opportunities, perhaps this could be something that happens sooner rather than later. Now we’ve written about this, perhaps this will manifest a Jets fumble return for a touchdown in an upcoming game. Otherwise, we’ll be writing about how long it was since Wilkerson’s touchdown again in a few seasons…

title: Scouting Jets offensive tackle Blake Freeland
summary: The Jets recently signed former Colts offensive lineman Blake Freeland to their active roster from the Bengals’ practice squad. Today, we break him down in detail. The 25-year old Freeland is listed at 6’7” and 302 pounds and was a fourth round pick out of BYU in 2023. He has started nine games in his […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - OCTOBER 29: Blake Freeland #73 of the Indianapolis Colts runs onto the field prior to the game against the New Orleans Saints at Lucas Oil Stadium on October 29, 2023 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jets recently signed former Colts offensive lineman Blake Freeland to their active roster from the Bengals’ practice squad. Today, we break him down in detail. The 25-year old Freeland is listed at 6’7” and 302 pounds and was a fourth round pick out of BYU in 2023. He has started nine games in his career, all of which were for the Colts in his rookie year. Background Freeland was a three-star high school recruit but headed to BYU with zero experience of playing on the offensive line having been a quarterback for two years before moving to tight end and defensive end as a senior. He also played basketball and represented his school in shot put and javelin throwing. On his arrival at BYU, Freeland converted to offensive tackle but didn’t see the field until the middle of his freshman season. However, he ended up starting the last seven games and held up reasonably well, as he only allowed one sack. He didn’t begin his sophomore year as a starter, but ended up making a total of eight starts in 2020, during which he showed promise by not allowing a sack all year. In 2021 and 2022, Freeland started all 26 games and was twice named to Phil Steele’s all-Independent Conference first team. He was also a third team AP all-American in 2022. Heading into the 2023 pre-draft process, Freeland was being touted as a possible day two pick. However, his rawness was exposed during Senior Bowl week. Even so, he managed to stablize his stock with good workouts at the combine and his pro day. The Colts eventually drafted Freeland in the fourth round and he started off his rookie year on the bench. He soon made his first start due to a week four injury, and by the end of the year had started nine games. In 2024, he failed to earn a starting role and spent the first half of the season as a healthy scratch. He played in the last eight games, although he only played 23 offensive snaps, 22 of which were in the season finale. In year three, a serious leg injury during preseason forced Freeland to spend the entire year on injured reserve and then he faced an uphill battle to make the team out of training camp this summer. After being released in final cuts following preseason, Freeland signed to Cincinnati’s practice squad before being poached by the Jets last month following Max Mitchell’s concussion. Let’s move onto some more in-depth analysis of what Freeland brings to the table, based on in-depth research and film study. Measurables/Athleticism Freeland is extremely tall, with excellent length, but was not strong enough when he entered the league so has no doubt been trying to add weight and is almost certainly heavier than his listed weight of 302. He managed 25 bench press reps at his pro day. The rest of his workout numbers are impressive as he ran the 40-yard dash in under five seconds at the combine, then broke the combine record for offensive linemen with a 37-inch vertical jump. His broad jump of 120 inches was also impressive. Having posted underwhelming agility numbers at the combine, Freeland did those drills again at his pro day and improved them dramatically. Usage Freeland has extensive experience of playing at both tackle positions. He started two seasons of each in college and has played both during his preseason appearances. At the NFL level, his first two starts were on the left but the other seven were on the right. He would not be suitable for an interior role and has never played there at any level. Pass Blocking Freeland only allowed two sacks in his entire college career, with a low pressure rate. However, BYU’s system operates with a lot of screens and RPO’s so he didn’t play as many true pass sets as you’d like to see from an incoming prospect. Not surprisingly, he struggled during his nine starts as a rookie, giving up four sacks. Talented NFL level players were always going to be able to exploit his lack of experience, and it didn’t help his confidence that he faced Aaron Donald in his first NFL start. Despite his athletic numbers, Freeland can sometimes be slow to get into his stance and susceptible to being beaten by speed rushers around the edge. However, his biggest concern is his anchor. He can really struggle to repel bull rushers and speed-to-power moves. Run Blocking Freeland’s run blocking grades according to Pro Football Focus were very good when he was in college, but he was less consistent at the NFL level. The 2023 season when Freeland played extensively for the Colts was Jonathan Taylor’s least productive of his career and he only had one 100-yard game which came on a day when Freeland didn’t play. Once again, play strength is an issue here, as he will get stood up on the edge and allow his man to fight off his block in the trenches. He does give a good effort though, and his athletic ability means he can get out in space to good effect. Short Yardage Freeland had some decent moments on short yardage plays, even though he’s not much of a drive blocker. It may suit him that effort is arguably more important than technique in such situations. Screen Blocking Freeland obviously has the athleticism to get out in front of a screen and, as noted, it was something BYU did regularly when he was there. Here’s a play where he was at right tackle. On this one, rather than leaking out, he has an initial responsibility to prevent the upfield rush but then finds someone to block so the play doesn’t get bottled up. Footwork/Technique Considering his speed and agility numbers, it is disappointing to see that Freeland is sometimes stiff and mechanical in his movements. One other obvious area that needs work is his hand placement. He can be slow to get his hands up and defensive players will take advantage of this. His other big issue is pad level. This was always going to be an issue for someone as tall as him and he can tend to play with a narrow base so is often overpowered. Penalties Freeland had seven penalties in seven games as a freshman but improved his on-field discipline over the course of his college career with just nine penalties in the last three seasons. At the NFL level, he’s been flagged six times. Four of these were false starts and two were for illegal man downfield. He has zero holding penalties. Special Teams Freeland’s only role on special teams in college was as a blocker on the placekicking unit and that has been the case in the NFL too. He has had no issues or penalties within this role. Instincts/Intelligence Freeland displayed good patience on stunts as a college player, and has shown he can handle those at the NFL level too. However, it’s in those one-on-one battles – especially as a pass rusher – where his lack of experience can be detrimental as he can be slow to react to or anticipate counters. Attitude Freeland is a player who is known for his toughness and a relentless work ethic. He also has good leadership traits, having been a three-time high school captain – he played two years as a quarterback, remember – and also a captain at BYU. Injuries To miss your entire third season having entered the NFL as someone who was considered a raw developmental prospect is rough luck and Freeland’s fractured leg in 2025 has obviously hurt his career. Prior to this, injuries weren’t an issue as he played in 44 games in his college career despite being a healthy scratch for the first seven weeks. Scheme Fit As noted, BYU’s scheme used a lot of screens and RPO’s and, as such, probably wasn’t ideal preparation for entering the NFL. However, Freeland has since had four camps with the Colts and spent a couple of months in Cincinnati this year. Although current Jets offensive coordinator Frank Reich left the Colts in 2022 and Freeland was drafted by them the…
